articles.title_orig: Leo XIV urges Church in China to honor culture and Rome
articles.title_zh: Leo XIV urges Church in China to honor culture and Rome
articles.content_orig:
Receive Aleteia every day in your inbox.
In his first message devoted to the Catholic Church in China, the Pope emphasized the importance of cultural identity and communion with Rome.
Pope Leo XIV called for a Church in China that is fully rooted in its culture while remaining united with Rome, in a video message shown on November 5, 2026, at a conference in Rome marking the centenary of the ordination of the first Chinese bishops of the modern era. It was the first address the Pope has devoted specifically to the Catholic Church in China since his election.
The conference, opened by Cardinal Secretary of State Pietro Parolin — the Vatican's second-highest-ranking official — marked 100 years since Pope Pius XI ordained six Chinese bishops on October 28, 1926. They had traveled by ship from Shanghai, making the long sea journey to Rome to receive episcopal ordination in St. Peter's Basilica.
At the entrance to the conference hall at the Pontifical Urbaniana University on Thursday, Cardinal Parolin greeted the two bishops who had come from China for the occasion: Archbishop Joseph Li Shan of Beijing, president of the Chinese Catholic Patriotic Association, an organization affiliated with the Communist Party that oversees Catholicism in China; and Bishop Ignatius Ding Zuyao of Haimen, who was recently appointed.
Around 100 people attended the gathering, including Cardinal Stephen Chow, Bishop of Hong Kong, and Cardinal Lazarus You Heung-sik of South Korea, prefect of the Dicastery for the Clergy. At the beginning of the conference, held under the auspices of the Dicastery for Evangelization, organizers announced that the Pope had sent them a video message, which was then shown on a large screen.
In his address, Leo XIV described the ordination of the six bishops a century ago as “an event of great significance, not only for the journey of the Catholic Church in China, but also for the universal Church.” Drawing on this historical event, he emphasized the importance of inculturation and the communion of bishops with Rome.
The Pontiff cited Pope Benedict XV , who taught in his 1919 apostolic letter Maximum illud that “the missionary work of the Church cannot be confused with processes of colonization and the exportation of ideas or cultural models.” Christian faith, Leo XIV explained, “embraces differences, incorporating, wherever possible, the characteristics of individuals and peoples, with a broad outlook.”
While the Church “lives among the peoples with friendship and sympathy for their hopes and noble aspirations,” the 267th pope emphasized the importance of communion between bishops around the world and the Successor of Peter, as well as with their fellow bishops.
He described this unity as “a beautiful sign, freely given, comforting, a liberating bond, a closeness that inspires confidence.” He also stressed “the uniqueness of the Church in comparison with all other social and political systems and organizations.”
To support his remarks, Leo XIV again cited Benedict XVI , who wrote that the Catholic Church in China “has never been deprived of the ministry of legitimate Pastors who have preserved the apostolic succession intact.” He also referred to a message from Pope Francis emphasizing the “communion with the Bishop of Rome” of Chinese Catholics.
In conclusion, the Pope recalled that the journey of the six Chinese bishops had “kindled joy and pride in so many of their compatriots, consigning mistrust, suspicion and hostility to oblivion.”
In a world “torn apart by conflicts and overwhelmed by wars,” he invited prayers that, in the face of every threat, “the Lord may safeguard the treasure of ecclesial communion.”
Since the signing of the 2018 agreement between China and the Holy See on the appointment of bishops, 21 episcopal appointments have been made under its framework, including seven by Leo XIV.

articles.title_orig: Berkshire shares surge as Wall Street swoons amid AI fears
articles.title_zh: Berkshire shares surge as Wall Street swoons amid AI fears
articles.content_orig:
(This is the Warren Buffett Watch newsletter, news and analysis on all things Warren Buffett and Berkshire Hathaway. You can sign up here to receive it every Friday evening in your inbox.)
Berkshire Hathaway shares roared past the S&P 500 index this week as investors moved money away from slumping tech stocks and moved into what appears to be the relative safety of a traditional conglomerate with relatively little exposure to artificial intelligence amid fears massive spending on data centers won't pay off .
One month ago, Berkshire's widely held B shares were underperforming the S&P by 13.6 percentage points for the year.
With help from three more record-high closes this week, Berkshire is now 5.8 percentage points ahead of the benchmark.
Berkshire was up more than 5% this week while the S&P fell almost 2.7%.
The contrast is even sharper with the Nasdaq Composite , which fell 3.4% on the week.
Thursday's especially heavy tech selling pushed the index down more than 10% below its most recent high in what is commonly referred to as a " correction ," but it did make up some of its lost ground Friday .
Two weeks ago, Berkshire's share prices completely erased all of the roughly 15% drop they suffered in the three months following Warren Buffett's surprise announcement at the 2025 shareholders meeting that he would step down as CEO at the end of that year.
Now they are up 6% from the record high closes they hit the Friday before Buffett's revelation on May 3, 2025.
Berkshire is not completely removed from the convulsions around AI.
Abel told us in early September he sees a " significant opportunity " ahead for Berkshire Hathaway Energy to provide electricity to data centers.
He also expected Berkshire would benefit from its big bet on Google parent Alphabet , saying he and Warren Buffett knew AI was "going to have a significant impact on America and businesses," and " we saw Google as a significant player . "
Now that investment is getting negative reviews this week as the stock slumps along with other companies related to AI.
As of the end of June, Berkshire reported it owned almost 106 million shares of Alphabet, including 28.6 million shares it bought directly from the company in June: $5 billion of its Class A shares (GOOGL) for $351.81 each and another $5 billion of Class C shares (GOOG) for $348.20 each.
They are around $284 per share now.
It bought another $7 billion of Alphabet shares on the open market during the second quarter, adding to the position it started building in last year's third quarter, an investment initiated by Warren Buffett .
Bloomberg suggests that "with cracks in the AI trade starting to show, Berkshire's sudden push [into AI] may appear ill-timed."
On June 30, the position had a market value of $37.8 billion and it was the third largest equity holding in Berkshire's portfolio.
Since then both the Class A and Class C shares have dropped by around 20% and the stake is now valued at $30.2 billion , falling behind Coca-Cola's $38.3 billion to the portfolio's #4 position.
(In just over a week, we'll find out whether Berkshire made any changes to its Alphabet position during the third quarter ending September 30.)
Bloomberg quotes CFRA Research analyst Cathy Seifert as saying, "I do think that part of this may be a conscious decision to increase their exposure. One has to ask the question though, is it a little late?"
But the article notes that "for dedicated value investors and longtime Berkshire observers, such jitters may not really matter," with Keefe Bruyette & Woods analyst Meyer Shields saying Abel probably sees bets on AI as a long-term wager on the technology's potential, in keeping with the "conservatism that you would expect at Berkshire Hathaway."
At Barron's , however, Andrew Bary sees what he estimates is a $3 billion loss on Alphabet as part of a "disappointing" long-term trend in Berkshire's stock choices
"The company hasn't created much value from stock picking during the current decade" even though the "S&P 500 has returned 150% since the end of 2019 and tech stocks have quadrupled."
While Berkshire's investments in five Japanese "trading houses ," Chevron , and Chubb have done well, "there have been plenty of losers or simply mediocre investments that have been closed out."
He cites Verizon , HP , Paramount (now Skydance) , General Motors , Constellation Brands , and Pool .
While he estimates Berkshire's Occidental Petroleum investment is up about 20% from what it paid, OXY is "far behind most energy stocks" amid this year's big increase in crude prices.
Bary also lists stocks that have continued to rise in price after Berkshire cut its stakes, with Apple being the worst offender.
That stake has been reduced by 75% since 2023 at what Bary calculates is an average selling price around $200 per share, well below AAPL's current $342.
Despite those sales, Apple is Berkshire's largest equity holding with a market value of $78 billion . The stock is up 1200% since Berkshire started buying it at the beginning of 2016, at a time when many thought the company had already seen its best days.
Bary thinks Abel will probably keep Berkshire's core equity investments but may concentrate more on his strengths going forward: improving Berkshire's operating companies and making new acquisitions.
His conclusion: "Barring a market rout, equity investing may not be central to Berkshire anymore.
"And if any new Berkshire holdings are revealed soon, it may not be a good idea to buy them. The record hasn't been great."
Berkshire Hathaway's disclosure that it had made a relatively small $27 million addition to its $4.1 billion Sirius XM position helped fuel an ongoing rally that lifted the satellite radio company's shares to a 52-week high this week.
On Thursday morning last week, Sirius XM reported a 14% increase in its Q3 free cash flow, 5,000 more self-pay subscribers, and it raised its 2026 full-year financial guidance.
The stock ended 4.9% higher that day at $28.67.
On Friday, Monday, and Tuesday, Berkshire bought more than 924 thousand shares at an average price of $29.10 as the stock continued to gain ground, ending Tuesday at $30.80.
Berkshire disclosed the buys late Tuesday evening, apparently helping to fuel an additional 8.4% gain as the stock closed at $33.40 on Wednesday.
It hit a 52-week intraday high of $33.76 on Thursday but finished lower Friday at $32.40.
Overall, Sirius XM is up 18.6% since the earnings release and has gained 62.0% so far this year.
It's the first addition to Berkshire's stake since late-July and early-August last year.
In 2025, it bought a total of 7.3 million shares at an average price of $21.86.
The position is likely one of portfolio manager Ted Weschler's stocks.
Pacific Power, a unit of Berkshire Hathaway's PacifiCorp, is asking California regulators for a 57% rate increase that would raise the typical residential electric bill by $120 a month.
The Wall Street Journal calls it a "stunning request even in an era of rising electricity costs."
The utility says the hike would be partially offset by a 14% decrease taking effect on January 1.
A lot of the $103 million that would be generated by the increase is already being spent on efforts to make power equipment in the sparsely populated and heavily wooded area more resistant to wildfires.
The utility is facing around $637 million in liability claims for fires in 2020 and 2022.
This week, Reuters reports , Oregon's Supreme Court heard arguments on whether to revive a jury verdict that could expose PacifiCorp "to tens of billions of dollars of potential damages over its role in four Oregon wildfires in 2020."

articles.title_orig: Paraguay: President Santiago Pena impeached, under house arrest over bank crisis
articles.title_zh: Paraguay: President Santiago Pena impeached, under house arrest over bank crisis
articles.content_orig:
Late night political drama as PeÃ±a is impeached and arrested
Paraguay's President Santiago PeÃ±a has been impeached and placed under house arrest after a bank collapse triggered a crisis that left more than half of the country's population without access to their accounts.
PeÃ±a was arrested on Friday minutes after lawmakers, including from his own party, unanimously voted to remove him from office following the collapse earlier this week of Ueno Bank, which has links to his private business interests.
He had offered to step down on Thursday. Rather than accept his resignation, senators impeached PeÃ±a and charged him with misconduct, meaning he has been stripped of the immunity usually granted to ex-presidents.
PeÃ±a, who until last year held shares in the company that owned the bank, has denied any wrongdoing.
The impeachment charges that led to PeÃ±a's removal alleged he had conflicts of interest, manipulated regulatory oversight, diverted pension funds, and participated in an institutional cover-up involving the central bank.
He is due to be questioned on Saturday over allegations of breach of trust, influence peddling, and misappropriation of funds, prosecutor Silvia Margarita Gonzalez Vester said.
PeÃ±a's deputy, Pedro Alliana, has been sworn in as the new interim president and promised not to "abandon" the millions of people affected by the scandal.
"Compatriots who are now going through a difficult time as a result of the financial collapse will be fully compensated," said Alliana, who will serve as president until 2028.
The demise of the digital bank left more than half of Paraguay's population without access to their savings after it was seized by Paraguay's central bank.
Long lines of people trying to withdraw money from Ueno branches snaked down the streets of the capital Asuncion on Tuesday and Wednesday.
An estimated three million depositors remain unable to access their savings and pensions, prompting public outrage particularly in the capital, AsunciÃ³n.
Protests erupted across the country in response, with thousands taking to the streets on Thursday to demand their money.
Earlier demonstrations featured clashes with the police, who used tear gas and water cannons on the crowd.
PeÃ±a's impeachment passed with 44 out of 45 senators voting in favour of it. One lawmaker was absent.
"It was never my intention to betray the trust you placed in me," PeÃ±a said in a video posted on X announcing his resignation, adding his priority was "the peace of mind of Paraguayans who entrusted their savings to our financial system".
Afterwards, senate president Basilio NÃºÃ±ez said PeÃ±a was found guilty of "dereliction of duty".
Pedro Alliana takes the oath of office as interim President
Senator Rafael Filizzola said: "We are facing the biggest corruption scandal in our democratic history â a tremendous blow to the state, to private citizens, and to the country's credibility and image."
Analysts say PeÃ±a is likely to now be prosecuted over the bank's collapse.
His defence lawyer Ricardo Preda described the allegations as a "reckless accusation" that was "irresponsible and opportunistic".

articles.title_orig: Conservative bloc takes a slim lead in New Zealand election that’s still too close to call
articles.title_zh: Conservative bloc takes a slim lead in New Zealand election that’s still too close to call
articles.content_orig:
New Zealand voters face weeks of political limbo after a knife-edge election left the country’s conservative coalition government at risk of losing its majority following just a single term in office.
Saturday’s preliminary results show Prime Minister Christopher Luxon’s National-led coalition with a two seat majority. But the margin is so tight, a small variance in the final tally could yet leave the opposition left-wing bloc with a chance to form a government.
Luxon told supporters gathered in Auckland that while it looked like his party had a pathway to form the next government, the race remained “too close to call.”
He said the country would need to wait until the Electoral Commission delivered the final official results on November 27 for certainty. Coalition negotiations could then drag on for weeks before a government is formed.
Preliminary numbers show the right-wing coalition grouping has 67 seats in the 131-seat parliament.
Should it fall short of a majority, Luxon would likely need to turn to the progressive centrist Opportunity party , which will enter parliament for first time, for support. Prior to the election he had ruled out working with the party.
The center-left Labour party received the highest share of the popular vote under the country’s mixed-member proportional voting system by a tiny margin, but a stronger performance in individual electorates has delivered National more seats in parliament.
Labour Leader Chris Hipkins made light of Saturday’s inconclusive results as he addressed supporters in Wellington, saying: “Tonight, New Zealand has spoken. It may take us a little bit longer to figure out exactly what it is that you’ve said.”
Hipkins – who served briefly as prime minister in 2023 –  did not concede, telling the crowd that “every vote matters. And every vote must be counted.”
The opposition grouping of center-left Labour, the leftist Greens and indigenous party Te Pati Māori is projected to have 57 seats. But the bloc could have a path to power if it picked up some additional seats in the final count, and if it secured the support of Opportunity.
The incumbent coalition – the country’s most right-wing in a generation – took power in 2023, capitalizing on an electorate looking for change in the wake of the Covid-19 pandemic.
But its struggle to secure an emphatic victory this time signifies the level of public discontent over living costs, stubbornly high unemployment rates and concerns over healthcare.
Luxon’s center-right National party emerges a diminished force, crashing to just 29.3% of the popular vote, down from 38% in 2023, according to the preliminary count.
Its coalition partners, the right-wing-libertarian ACT party and the nationalist New Zealand First Party, increased their vote share to 11% and 10% respectively, putting them both in a stronger position to dictate terms in pending coalition talks.
The stronger-than-expected result for New Zealand First and ACT, and National’s weakened position, raises the prospect of the coalition moving further to the right in a second term and further embracing culture-war policies.
On the campaign trail the ACT vowed to end affirmative action schemes at the country’s medical schools, while New Zealand First promised sweeping immigration changes and voiced support for a review of the ban on gay conversion therapy.
Luxon, would also have a complex job filling key cabinet posts in a second term, with a raft of senior lawmakers from his National party, including finance minister Nicola Willis and parliament’s speaker Gerry Brownlee, losing their seats.
Swing voters turned away from National and Labour, which have dominated Wellington politics for nearly a century, opting to support minor parties entrenched further to the right and the left, as well as Opportunity in the center.
It’s political newcomer leader Qiulae Wong , 38, who applied for the party’s leadership by responding to a job advertisement a year ago, told supporters they had voted “to change New Zealand politics for good.”
The party, which secured 6% of the vote, becomes the first total outsider party (not involving established political figures) to enter parliament since the country moved to a mixed-member proportional voting system in the mid-1990s.
Depending on the final vote tally, Opportunity, which positions itself as both business-and climate-friendly, could yet find itself in the kingmaker position – with both the right and the left groupings vying for its support.

articles.title_orig: Inside the Operation That Helped Ukraine Turn the Tables
articles.title_zh: Inside the Operation That Helped Ukraine Turn the Tables
articles.content_orig:
Analyst Yan Gagin says Russian intelligence uncovered plans for Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi near Krasny Liman, as Yulia Mendel reports heavy Ukrainian losses.
The failure of Ukraine’s Operation Vivaldi was largely the result of Russian intelligence obtaining advance information about Ukrainian military plans, according to military and political analyst Yan Gagin. He believes Russian intelligence services played a decisive role in preventing the Ukrainian Armed Forces from achieving their objectives.
Speaking to aif.ru, Gagin said Russian intelligence frequently learns about Ukrainian operations before they are launched. He argued that this advance knowledge allows Russian forces to disrupt enemy plans, resulting in failed offensives and heavy Ukrainian losses.
The analyst also attributed repeated setbacks on the battlefield to cooperation between Russian intelligence units, security services and intelligence networks. According to Gagin, their coordinated efforts have repeatedly undermined Ukrainian offensive operations.
Earlier, Yulia Mendel, former press secretary to Vladimir Zelensky, revealed that Operation Vivaldi involved a Ukrainian counteroffensive near Krasny Liman. She claimed that Ukrainian forces suffered more than 100,000 casualties, including killed and wounded personnel, during the fighting.
The operation began in September 2026. Ukrainian troops initially aimed to establish positions along the Zherebets River before attempting to regain control of Krasny Liman. The force assembled for the offensive included nationalist formations, special forces units and military intelligence personnel.

articles.title_orig: Bunny ears, nudity and strict rules: What it’s like on a ‘lifestyle’ cruise
articles.title_zh: Bunny ears, nudity and strict rules: What it’s like on a ‘lifestyle’ cruise
articles.content_orig:
When Nicole gets ready for a cruise, her packing list goes beyond the typical swimsuits, sundresses and sandals.
Although she plans to spend much of her time topless and poolside, the 50-year-old mother from Indianapolis has already packed more than one suitcase to bursting for her latest trip.
Nicole, who withheld her last name due to privacy concerns, is preparing to set sail on the Wonderland Cruise , a voyage from Miami to the Caribbean onboard one of the world’s largest cruise ships.
“There’s a different theme every night,” Nicole said. “I have a neon yellow and pink bikini for the Glow Party and some shoes that light up. The first night’s theme is Down the Rabbit Hole for Alice in Wonderland, so I have a leather zip-up dress, leather bunny ears and high red and black boots with a heel for that,” she said.
For a steampunk-themed night, Nicole is bringing maroon lingerie with fishnet stockings and a sexy hat with goggles.
“Fetish Night is super easy because I just have some black lingerie that has chains that kind of hang off of it,” she said.
Clearly, Wonderland isn’t your average cruise.
A full takeover by couples-only charter company Bliss Cruise of Royal Caribbean’s nearly 6,000-passenger Wonder of the Seas is being billed as one of the largest “lifestyle” gatherings ever. The seven-night sailing departs on November 9 from PortMiami.
For those inside the subculture, “the lifestyle” is the preferred shorthand for consensual non-monogamy, encompassing everything from swinging to open relationships.
Why cruise ships are sailing to a phantom destination that doesn’t appear on any map
Nicole, who participates in the lifestyle and cruising with her husband of 27 years, says that meeting up with friends from previous Bliss Cruise sailings and making new ones at sea and in port calls like Curaçao and Aruba will be a key part of the week’s fun.
“We always joke with people and say it’s like the high school reunion that you want to go to,” she said.
For some, lifestyle cruises answer a call of the wild and offer the chance to let loose at sea beyond the usual casino tables, ice skating spectacles, waterslides and snorkeling excursions.
It’s a tourism sector that appears to be growing. While cruise industry organization Cruise Lines International Association did not respond to CNN Travel’s questions about this charter-cruise niche, “lifestyle” cruisers have noted more options on larger ships.
“What we’re seeing today is a not just a growth in the number of (lifestyle cruise) brands, but a significant increase in the size of the boats they occupy,” said Mickey Gordon, who hosts the podcast Casual Swinger . Gordon, who also uses a pseudonym for privacy reasons, said that while lifestyle cruises used to be niche events with 800 or so travelers, today’s ships are some of the largest at sea, easily selling out with 5,000 guests or more at a time.
And the reason these cruises are so popular is simple, Gordon said.
“There is simply nowhere on earth you can go that has more ‘people like me’ than a lifestyle cruise. That fact alone sells the trip,” he said.
The Wonderland Cruise, which has been sold out since March 2026 , says it will welcome 5,802 registered guests, all 21 and older, onboard Wonder of the Seas.
They hail predominantly from the United States, which accounts for 87% of bookings, followed by Canada and other nations. Bliss Cruise said guests from 47 countries will be aboard.
Passengers on the cruise represent a near-even split between male and female guests. It’s a requirement that each cabin has at least one man and one woman. “Throuples,” in this case three people with at least one man and woman among them, are permitted to share a cabin (foursomes with two women and two men, while rare, are also allowed). Just over half of passengers on the Wonderland Cruise are between the ages of 45 and 59, according to the company.
Super-sized cruise ships are becoming the norm. Is there an end in sight?
Cabin rates for bookings made in December 2024 ranged between $1,630 per person for interior cabins and more than $21,000 per person for the Royal Loft Suite.
“We do a full charter of the entire ship. We essentially buy the cruise from the cruise line, and then we market that as a specialized lifestyle cruise charter,” Russell Stephens, the CEO of Bliss Cruise, told CNN Travel.
Despite popular misconceptions about lifestyle events, he said the goal isn’t an uninhibited free-for-all, but rather creating a secure, judgment-free space for open-minded couples.
“I think people can expect a lot of fun, and it’s not what some people would perhaps expect,” said Stephens, who said he is in “the lifestyle.”
“It’s really about providing a sex-positive experience for open-minded people,” he said.
Like many major cruises, Bliss has its own app that registered passengers can access before their vacation to browse the hour-by-hour activities offered each day of the cruise, communicate with other guests who have RSVPed for the same events and create personal pages similar to dating profiles.
Categories like “life Interests” — with options as benign as boating, cars, reading, cooking and parenting — are followed by “sex interests,” including dirty talk, massage and hot wife (“a married or partnered woman who engages in consensual sexual relationships with other people — typically men — with the full knowledge, consent, and often encouragement of her primary partner”), among others that are far more risqué.
The cruise’s app details workshops and seminars, many of which cost an additional fee and are already sold out. These range from relatively tame breathwork courses and speed dating sessions to kink and fetish workshops.
There are multiple daily meet-and-greets at bars and other ship venues, too, for people who fall into categories such as Under 45, Over 45, French, Veterans, Sober & Sexy, Silver & Sexy (seniors) and Hall Pass, which is described in the app as not a pass “to have sex in the hallways,” but rather “permission from your partner to engage in sexual activity without your partner being present.”
Meeting and talks geared toward newbies are also plentiful.
“There are a lot of workshops around just being new to the lifestyle and what that is,” Stephens said. “So we try to cater for people, and we really try to welcome newbies into the lifestyle. It’s sort of like they want to think about it, they’re dipping their toes into it, they’ve kind of had a fantasy or whatever. But maybe they’ve never done anything.
“We don’t want people like deer in the headlights,” when they come onboard, he said.
Bliss Cruise is not the only operator catering to lifestyle voyagers.
Other major players include Desire Cruises , a couples-only option with sailings in the Caribbean, the Mediterranean and Adriatic Seas, Asia and North Africa. LLV Club sells lifestyle cruise itineraries in places like Fiji and Tahiti along with South Korea and Japan. Killing Kittens also offers options on the high seas.
On land, there are hotels aimed at the lifestyle-curious and veterans alike, such as Hedonism II in Jamaica, where the mantra is “Be Wicked for a Week.”
‘The Love Boat’: How a TV show transformed the cruise industry
Lifestyle vacations attract a wide cross-section of society, Stephens said. Desire passengers who were interviewed by CNN Travel agreed.
“We’ve met CEOs, we’ve met housewives, we’ve met people in real estate, people who work for the National Security Agency, lots of lawyers and doctors, hotel owners, a math teacher and crazy rich Asians,” said Alice, a physician from the New York City area who has been on two Desire cruises with her husband Bob, a doctor. (The couple spoke under pseudonyms to protect their privacy.)
Alice and Bob are in their early 50s and have been married for 29 years. They first dipped their toes in at a lifestyle resort in the Caribbean in 2019 and are booked on their third Desire cruise, from Lisbon to Morocco, in 2027.

articles.title_orig: Trump’s midterm drubbing adds to the populist right’s losses. France’s Le Pen could still win
articles.title_zh: Trump’s midterm drubbing adds to the populist right’s losses. France’s Le Pen could still win
articles.content_orig:
European far-right leaders quick to distance themselves from US president and stress their own priorities
Europe live – latest updates
US midterms live – latest updates
The historic Republican defeat in the US midterm elections has forcibly reminded Europe’s far-right leaders of their perennial Donald Trump dilemma: they may love his nativist agenda, but the man himself is a toxic electoral liability.
Since his re-election in 2024, European populist leaders such as Marine Le Pen in France and Giorgia Meloni in Italy have carefully calibrated their public postures towards the US president, walking a delicate transatlantic tightrope.
They adore his policies on hard borders, culture wars and anti-globalism. But European voters, even on the far right , detest Trump’s personal volatility, geopolitical unpredictability, unreliability on Europe’s defence, and trade protectionism.
Trump’s territorial threats over Greenland and economic nationalism have proved particular problems: no leader who champions national sovereignty and domestic jobs could back threats to invade the largely self-governing territory of an EU member state or punitive trade tariffs.
The sheer scale of Tuesday’s Republican wipeout has now prompted Europe’s populists to distance themselves yet further while taking away one big lesson: angry, economically squeezed voters topple incumbents.
Across European capitals on Wednesday, far-right politicians were actively insulating themselves from the White House, while dutifully avoiding any personal attacks.
Jordan Bardella, the leader of the National Rally (RN) in France and a possible prime minister if Le Pen wins next year’s presidential ballot, led the charge. Without naming the president who ordered them, Bardella blamed the US attacks on Iran, which he said had carried “very heavy consequences” for world economies.
In Germany, Alice Weidel, a co-leader of Alternative für Deutschland, said Trump had promised his voters “not to pursue an interventionist foreign policy” and that “this broken campaign promise has now come back to haunt the Republicans”.
In Italy , Roberto Vannacci, the founder of the insurgent far-right National Future party, also said the result showed the political dangers of failing to deliver on electoral promises. “Trump failed to live up to expectations,” he said.
In Madrid, the Vox leader, Santiago Abascal, dumped all pretence of a Washington connection, brushing off questions about an ideological alliance by saying he was “in Spain , not in Michigan” and cared “quite little about what happens in other places”.
Mujtaba Rahman, of the Eurasia Group consultancy, said all were acting for domestic advantage, hoping still to benefit from the “ideological momentum of Trumpism” without being tarred by the “chaos and economic disruption of his presidency”.
For far-right parties in opposition, however, the US midterms offer a clear playbook: mounting public anger over rising prices and unaffordable housing can be channelled into electoral victory. That is clearly the hope of the National Rally in France .
Bardella has repeatedly said purchasing power and the cost of living would be “the absolute priority” of an RN government, with plans to cut VAT on electricity, gas and fuel and allow employers to boost wages without additional payroll charges.
In Spain, Vox is similarly weaponising soaring living costs and plunging housing affordability against the Socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, in hopes of entering government as partner in a rightwing coalition after elections on 29 November.
after newsletter promotion
For populist leaders already in power in Europe, such as Meloni, that is not good news. The Italian prime minister has already faced several waves of domestic protest in Rome, Milan and elsewhere, some of them violent, over fuel costs and inflation.
Her coalition partner Matteo Salvini, leader of the far-right League, conceded that the US vote was “influenced above all by the wars, international tensions and the increase in the cost of living, the consequences of which fall directly on families”.
Opposition MPs were equally quick to connect the dots, noting that Trump had pledged to lower prices and bring back quality jobs, but that never happened. And once in power, far-right leaders who fail to deliver are as vulnerable to voter anger as any others.
Some on the European far right, such Dan Dungaciu of Romania’s AUR, sought to play down Trump’s crushing defeat by arguing that reports of his “political death” were greatly exaggerated, but the broader political lesson may go beyond the populists.
The electoral fortunes of Europe’s far right, whose nationalist leaders will in all probability continue espousing Maga’s ideas while keeping Trump himself at arm’s length, do not depend on the success or failure of the US president at the ballot box.
The underlying grievances driving the rise of European populism – the cost of living, the housing crises, the rural-urban divide, arguments about immigration – are rooted firmly in European domestic conditions, not in American election results.
Some warn the worst consequence of these midterms would be for Europe’s mainstream parties to assume they showed the populist tide was receding. What they actually showed was that voter anger over the cost of living is unforgiving – whoever is in power.

articles.title_orig: Hackers probed Europe’s fridge systems weeks before cyberattacks. Who did it and what could they target next?
articles.title_zh: Hackers probed Europe’s fridge systems weeks before cyberattacks. Who did it and what could they target next?
articles.content_orig:
Cybersecurity researchers say they detected hackers probing internet-connected refrigeration systems across Europe in the days before a wave of cyberattacks and incidents disrupted supermarkets and blood banks, with evidence suggesting it may have been part of a coordinated operation.
Refrigeration systems in supermarkets across nine European countries as well as several blood banks in France were attacked on 2 and 3 November.
Hackers exploited weak cybersecurity and vulnerabilities in manufacturer Danfoss’s AK-SM refrigeration system manager to put fridges and freezers on defrost settings, in some cases temperatures were set as high 50 degrees Celsius.
The incidents forced many grocery stores to throw away spoiled produce from their fridges and freezers and have become a very visible example of how easily cyberattacks can disrupt everyday life by targeting infrastructure systems that are often taken for granted.
For cybersecurity firm Lupovis, the signs point to a coordinated operation potentially involving a state actor — one that was preceded by days of probing.
The company says it saw a period of reconnaissance targeting these systems just days before the attacks.
The company observed over 276 attempts coming from 91 different threat actors matching specific components of Danfoss controllers during this 10-day period. Activity peaking on 26 October, before coming to a halt at the end of the month.
“Between the 20th and 30th of October, what we saw was a wave of what we call reconnaissance,” CEO Xavier Bellekens told Euronews Next.
“We see a huge peak suddenly for 10 days where adversaries are trying the default passwords. They are trying a couple of those vulnerabilities.”
Lupovis operates a system of so-called “honeypots”, which replicate its clients’ online systems and technologies. The company equips them with sensors and then deliberately exposes them to hackers, encouraging attacks so it can track how these systems are accessed and exploited.
This intelligence can then be used to identify vulnerabilities without putting the clients' real systems at risk.
It was through this system that Lupovis, whose clients include the Scottish government, Orange, Telefonica and a number of retail companies, detected what it describes as “reconnaissance” on Danfoss systems in the days before November’s attacks.
“You can think of it as like burglars, driving through your neighbourhood and identifying the houses they are going to go and break into,” said Bellekens.
Lupovis then traced what it describes as the digital "breadcrumbs" left by the probing and attacks, finding that so-called "bulletproof hosting" was used — web hosting services that are designed to resist takedown requests and law enforcement intervention.
“On the one hand, you have Amazon Web Services, they are the opposite of a bullet-proof hosting. If you do something malicious with one of their servers, that's it, they cancel your account. Bulletproof hosting is the opposite. You do something malicious, It's out of jurisdiction," Bellekens said.
Lupovis then examined the hosting providers themselves.
“We realised that some of those bulletproof hosting had been used by Russian groups in the past,” says Bellekens.
The company is clear that just because servers are located somewhere does not necessarily mean that the people using it share the same nationality, so they cannot say for sure that Russia is behind the attacks.
“However, there's a bit of a pattern here,” says the Lupovis CEO, “So we are looking for someone that has the capability to attack certain countries in particular.”
According to the CEO, Lupovis sensors in South America, Africa, North America and Asia did not record the same activity. It was only picked up by sensors in Europe.
He also believes the ability to coordinate attacks across Europe helps narrow down the list of suspects.
“You [the attacker] have to be able to coordinate this attack because most of it happened within a 24-hour period.”
“All of this makes us point to an adversary that, to us, is not a script kiddie [an unskilled amateur]. They are not a lone wolf. It looks like a well-planned operation. So a state fits the bill.”
“When we pull on the thread it does look like it could well be Russia. So, that is basically where we're at.”
The incidents come amid wider concerns about hybrid threats and suspected Russian-linked activity targeting European countries.
However, the precise identity and motivation of the attackers remain unclear.
George Nott, technology editor at The Grocer, said the attacks appeared to have relied on relatively basic security weaknesses rather than highly advanced hacking techniques.
"Attackers managed to access refrigeration systems by simply finding their log-in pages on the open internet, and exploiting already patched vulnerabilities and weak passwords rather than some highly advanced technology," he told Euronews Next.
Nott also cautioned against drawing firm conclusions about who was responsible.
"it's still unclear who was behind the attack or what they hoped to achieve. We'll have to face the fact we may never known. With no ransom demand or claim of responsibility, it could have been anyone from a state-sponsored actor to a gang of teenagers 'doing it for the lols'."
Cybersecurity agencies in the countries affected this week have differed in how they describe the incidents. Belgium, Luxembourg, Italy, Portugal and Estonia have called them a “cyberattack”, while Sweden and Ireland referred to it as a “cyber incident”.
The European Union’s Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) has also stopped short of explicitly calling the incidents a cyberattack.
Hackers were able to access refrigeration systems across Europe because controller boxes connected to the internet were being used to remotely manage refrigeration units, Bellekens said.
Remote control of such devices is common in today’s increasingly digital world. However, the Lupovis CEO says many of the systems could have been better protected had they been placed on virtual private networks (VPNs) rather than exposed directly to the internet.
“[It] would have entirely mitigated the risk because like a VPN is more complex to exploit," he said.
To make matters worse, many of the systems were reportedly accessible using factory-default credentials, such as "Username" Supervisor" and "Password: 12345", suggesting that basic security measures had not been implemented.
Nott said the problem reflets a wider tendency in the retail sector to overlook the security of connected equipment.
“The security of connected equipment across the retail sector can overlooked — the priority given to more obvious targets such as payment systems and customer data," he said.
Once hackers had gained access to the refrigeration control systems they were able to switch them to defrost mode and ramp up the temperatures, spoiling goods stored in fridges and freezers across Europe.
The attacks have raised concerns about the security of other internet-connected equipment, from supermarket machinery to the systems that control access, heating and ventilation in buildings.
Nott warned the future attacks may not be confined to refrigeration systems.
"more and more of the systems that keep supermarkets running — heating, ventilation and air conditioning systems; electronic shelf labels; floor cleaning robots — could all present similar vulnerabilities if remote access isn't properly secured and software patched," he said.
But the potential exposure goes well beyond retail.
"The freezer is not special. It is just the most visible example of a much bigger category,” says Kumar Sokka, CEO of Acre Security, a global provider of integrated physical security.
“The same kind of small, internet-connected controller that was used to warm up those fridges also runs the doors, the access-control readers, the cameras, the alarms, the lighting and the heating and ventilation in most modern buildings.”

articles.title_orig: Powerful Haitian gang reaches out to state disarmament group as gunfights persist
articles.title_zh: Powerful Haitian gang reaches out to state disarmament group as gunfights persist
articles.content_orig:
Soldiers may end up in ferocious battles across sprawling slums, say experts who question Nayib Bukele’s motive
I t has been nearly five years since El Salvador’s authoritarian leader, Nayib Bukele, launched his controversial “war” on gangs – transforming his country’s fortunes and becoming a hard-right beacon for Latin America’s fight against violent crime.
Now the Salvadoran populist seems intent on exporting his hardline tactics to the region’s most violence-stricken nation, Haiti. He has sent more than 2,000 troops and special forces to the Caribbean country since four citizens of El Salvador were abducted there on 18 October.
“We will help you reclaim your country from the hands of the traitors who betrayed the legacy of Dessalines,” Bukele tweeted in Haitian Creole this week, in reference to one of the leaders of the Haitian Revolution, Jean-Jacques Dessalines.
Bukele’s use of mass incarceration and secret negotiations to tame El Salvador’s gangs has made him a hero among rightwing politicians and violence-weary citizens across the Americas , including in Haiti, where heavily armed groups have commandeered much of the capital, Port-au-Prince, since President Jovenel Moïse was murdered in 2021.
Experts say many Haitians welcome the idea of a Bukele-style crackdown, even if El Salvador and Haiti are dramatically different places.
Vanda Felbab-Brown, a Haiti security expert from the Brookings Institution in Washington, said: “Right now, the conditions in Haiti are so awful that there’s a huge craving for a strongman who [can] deliver Haiti from the gangs. People are desperate and they want whoever will stop the desperation. ”
In recent days a large number of pro-Bukele allies and boosters with huge social media followings have gone online to hail his Haiti intervention.
“He’s single-handedly going to clean up the entire Caribbean. I wish more political leaders had balls like this,” claimed one cheerleader , alongside images of rifle-toting Salvadoran soldiers on the streets of Port-au-Prince.
Others posted footage of crowds of Haitians celebrating the troops’ arrival, although there have been reports of protests against the deployment.
There are also widespread concerns over Bukele’s foreign foray – the first the region has seen in many years, outside a UN mission – with mystery shrouding its true objectives. There are fears it could fuel the already devastating levels of bloodshed and aggravate a humanitarian crisis in which more than 1.5 million citizens have been forced to flee their homes.
When the four Salvadorans – who Bukele said were aviation technicians – vanished after going shopping in a gang-run area north-east of Port-au-Prince’s airport, El Salvador’s president initially painted his military operation as a rescue mission.
“We have a single objective: to bring our four compatriots back home alive,” he wrote on X, demanding their release. “We have already destroyed the gangs in El Salvador, and we can finish you off too,” he warned their kidnappers.
But over the following days, Bukele’s tweets began to suggest more ambitious goals. “We came to Haiti to fight against the wicked,” the social media-savvy leader wrote.
In another post, he denied he was stumbling into a Caribbean version of the Battle of Waterloo, when Napoleon Bonaparte’s dreams of imperial glory were finally crushed. “God will grant us victory. The Creator of the Universe is with us,” Bukele insisted.
Felbab-Brown said those posts indicated his objectives were broad and involved “degrading the gangs”, rather than simply rescuing his four citizens – or more likely, given the brutality of Haiti’s gangs, their bodies.
It is unclear how long Bukele’s troops plan to stay, although they are setting up a base near the US embassy, suggesting a quick exit is unlikely.
Adam Isacson, a security specialist from the Washington Office on Latin America, said the nature and scope of Bukele’s security and military strategies were obscure. “But the political strategy is pretty clear,” he added.
Isacson believes the Salvadoran leader’s intervention is partly about burnishing his crime-busting credentials before February’s presidential election in El Salvador and partly an attempt to enhance his reputation as Latin America’s premier rightwing security wizard.
Felbab-Brown agreed. “It’s possible he’s trying to strengthen his hero image in Latin America and show that he can do what he did in El Salvador beyond El Salvador ,” she said, noting how the Central American country faced “real economic headwinds” that posed a challenge as Bukele sought to extend his seven-year rule.
Experts do not rule out the possibility of Bukele dealing a blow to the gangs – in the short term at least – but say the risks are immense.
Already, a volatile constellation of armed groups is operating on the ground in Haiti trying to subdue gang fighters – so far with limited success.
It includes vigilante mobs armed with guns and machetes, the Haitian police and army, foreign mercenaries employed by Vectus Global , a firm owned by Erik Prince – who founded the controversial private military contractor Blackwater – and a UN-backed mission called the Gang Suppression Force (GSF), led by a Mongolian army general.
Bukele’s soldiers, who are not operating under the command of the GSF, have now entered that messy fray.
“It is an orchestra without a conductor,” warned Romain Le Cour, who runs the Haiti Observatory at the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime and is a regular visitor to Port-au-Prince.
One major risk is escalation. “With drones, attack helicopters and heavy weapons, the confrontation has changed dramatically in a matter of days,” Le Cour said. “Civilians are paying the price. This is urban guerrilla-type combat, where residents are trapped between criminal groups and intensive operations. Thousands have already been displaced.”
Felbab-Brown said that, depending on their approach, Salvadoran forces could become embroiled in ferocious man-to-man fighting in sprawling slums.
“Maybe there will be luck and you will have ‘big bang’ initial operations that will scare the gangs into negotiations … but one can also imagine really, really, really tough urban fighting,” she said.
Civilian losses are a major concern, particularly given the indiscriminate nature of Bukele’s incarceration campaign in El Salvador, where tens of thousands of people have been jailed since he declared a state of emergency in March 2022, many without any proven links to gangs .
“Will the Salvadoran force operate with great effectiveness and great precision and be highly discriminating between civilians and gangs in a way that Bukele has not been in El Salvador ?” Felbab-Brown asked.
Le Cour said another risk was that Haiti could become a deadly quagmire for Salvadoran troops who lacked reliable intelligence and were unfamiliar with the terrain.
Bill O’Neill, the UN’s expert on human rights in Haiti, said: “​It’s all very opaque and unpredictable … it potentially ​[could get] very ugly and very dangerous. I hope it doesn’t turn out that way​ – but I just don’t know​.”
Donald Trump this week offered support for Bukele’s mission, telling reporters he had spoken to his ally about the deployment of troops, some of whom flew to Port-au-Prince on a US military plane .
“He said that he has a big problem with Haiti. I said: ‘Look, you’re running your country. You have to do what you have to do,’” the American president said, claiming US help was not necessary because Bukele was “in pretty good shape”.
Le Cour suspected Haiti “might be a laboratory … for a new way of intervening in different places in the hemisphere, with a proxy country doing it with the green light of Washington”.

World of Warcraft is the game that absolutely refuses to die, and in fact, it's potentially now bigger than ever.
Confirmed today on the official Warcraft social media channels, Blizzard said that World of Warcraft Forever represents its biggest launch in history by peak players, beating even the likes of Wrath of the Lich King from WoW's previous height almost two decades ago.
"Congratulations, you made HISTORY!" the post reads, "WoW: Forever has achieved the biggest launch in WoW history by peak concurrent players," and also confirmed that it has "the highest number of returning WoW players in history" as well.
Congratulations everyone, you made HISTORY!
WoW: Forever has achieved:
🔹The biggest launch in WoW history by peak concurrent players
🔹The highest number of returning players in WoW history
This is all because of you, the players. From all of us, THANK YOU! https://t.co/MQxQXmNDbA November 7, 2026
For those who don't know, World of Warcraft is an MMORPG where thousands of players pile into single servers to create a persistent, online living world. Microsoft and Xbox acquired the game a few years ago along with Activision , Blizzard, and King, and it has already been teasing a World of Warcraft port to Xbox consoles for some time. The game is presently only available on PC and cloud streaming services like NVIDIA GeForce Now.
The retail version of World of Warcraft has strayed intensely from the game's original vision in recent years, leading to players leaving the game and potentially even the genre en masse . World of Warcraft Forever is essentially a remix and polish of the original vision for World of Warcraft, with minimal handholding, a boosted sense of risk and reward, a reduction in "convenience" features that reduce in-game social interaction, atop a boost in visual quality. WoW:F also has thousands of new quests and stories, taking place in an "alternative timeline" of sorts that exists a year or so before World of Warcraft's original base game.
It remains to be seen if WoW:F can maintain the momentum it has seen, but the whole ordeal leaves World of Warcraft's main arm, currently dubbed Midnight, with a bit of a headache in my view.
Many games have tried to kill World of Warcraft over the years, but none have truly succeeded. WoW and Final Fantasy 14 remain the only large, populated purely subscription-based MMORPGs at least in the West as of writing, with incumbents relying on free-to-play business models to entice players.
World of Warcraft's subscription model ensures it can pump out huge amounts of content at a rapid clip, although in recent years, many have been wondering if it has become too rapid. World of Warcraft's main "retail" arm has seen a huge decline in quality , with players asking the firm to slow down to focus on the details and polish. Blizzard so far has ignored those calls.
WoW:F represents a complete reversal on what WoW retail has become in essence. World of Warcraft retail has abandoned all forms of immersion, friction, world building, and outdoor levelling gameplay for a focus on arcade-style endgame content which, while admittedly still fun, is frankly quite exhausting. World of Warcraft's story writing has been dismal for years, and bugs have been more prevalent than ever before.
RELATED: World of Warcraft's Ion Hazzikostas promises Retail won't get abandoned
The WoW:F team exists separately from the WoW: Retail team, and the divergence in philosophies are stark. WoW:F's focus on social systems, in-game immersion, understated and environmental storytelling, and slower, more methodical gameplay seems far more inline with what lapsed WoW players actually want.
I feel World of Warcraft's retail arm has focused on "data telemetry" over good human design instincts and it has led to the game's hollowing out. Hopefully, World of Warcraft: Forever can give Blizzard a hard lesson in listening to players directly — something I feel the retail team no longer does.

Jez is known for breaking exclusive news and analysis as relates to the Microsoft ecosystem — while being powered by tea. Follow on X.com/JezCorden and tune in to the XB2 Podcast , all about, you guessed it, Xbox!

articles.title_orig: After the US midterm rout of Trumpism, the world struggles to trust America again
articles.title_zh: After the US midterm rout of Trumpism, the world struggles to trust America again
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 3, the day of the midterm elections. Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
One thing is clear from this week's midterm elections: The Trump administration's foreign policy decisions were no longer just about what happened abroad. The war in Iran has driven up gas prices, while Trump's tariffs have raised costs for American businesses.
According to the Voter Poll conducted by SSRS for several news outlets, including The Associated Press, 51% of voters said U.S. support for Israel had been too strong, while 63% said the war in Iran was the wrong decision. Nearly three-quarters (74%) considered the war a major or crucial factor in their vote. The economy weighed even more heavily, with 89% calling it a major or crucial factor.
And while Americans were making their views known at the ballot box, the rest of the world had plenty to say, too. Sometimes with a little more humor. The election results have inspired AI-generated videos, social media memes and newspaper headlines abroad.
What could the results actually change?
Anne Applebaum, a Pulitzer Prize-winning historian and staff writer at The Atlantic , has spent years studying authoritarianism and the erosion of democratic institutions. In a February interview with NPR, she warned about corruption in U.S. foreign policy , saying people around Trump and his family had accepted money from foreign governments and others.
Now, with Democrats set to control Congress, Applebaum sees reason for U.S. allies to regain some confidence in American democracy. But whether that translates into changes in foreign policy is another question.
On Morning Edition, Applebaum outlined three ways Congress could influence U.S. foreign policy, from the war in Iran to Ukraine, and where its power would stop. Read her takeaways below.
1. How Congress could influence the war in Iran
The U.S. and Israel have carried out military campaigns against Iran since June 2025. The war has cost American taxpayers an estimated $47.1 billion as of mid-October, according to Pentagon figures obtained by The Associated Press . Iranian retaliatory strikes have also targeted U.S. military bases in the Gulf.
"I don't expect Trump to change," Applebaum said. "He's not that interested in what Americans think of his policies."
There is also a question of timing. Iran remains wary of renewed attacks , and some supporters of the war may see the next two months, before the new Congress takes office, as their last chance to escalate the conflict, Trita Parsi, an Iran expert at the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, told NPR's Hadeel Al-Shalchi.
Once Democrats take control of both chambers, they could use one of Congress's most important powers: deciding how federal money is spent. Lawmakers can seek restrictions in spending bills that would limit the use of federal funds for certain military operations.
"You could see them trying to use the power of the purse, the appropriations committees, to end the war or to influence politics," Applebaum said.
She expects that pressure to "change the trajectory of the war sooner or later."
2. What congressional investigations could reveal
Congress can also investigate how the administration makes foreign policy decisions, even when it cannot directly reverse them.
Applebaum expects lawmakers to examine potential corruption involving people close to Trump and decisions made by his foreign policy team. She raised questions about Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's competence and the advice Trump received during the Iran war.
Such investigations could bring more information into public view, but they would not necessarily produce a change in policy.
"Congress can't force the president to make changes," Applebaum said, noting that Trump can veto legislation.
Congress could, however, offer "a different narrative, both about this war and more broadly about American foreign policy," she said.
For that to matter, Applebaum said, Democratic leaders would need to move quickly, decide what to investigate and establish their priorities.
3. What could change for Ukraine
Support for Ukraine has crossed party lines in Congress, even as the Trump administration's approach to Russia has raised questions among lawmakers.
Applebaum expects that bipartisan coalition to become more active under Democratic control, including through legislation that would require the president to reimpose sanctions on Russia.
"I would expect legislation forcing the president to reimpose sanctions," she said.
The question is whether enough lawmakers would support such legislation to override a presidential veto. Applebaum said she could not predict that outcome, though she considered it possible given the level of congressional support for Ukraine.
Congress has already sought answers about disruptions to Ukraine's satellite communications. In October, the Pentagon's inspector general declined a bipartisan request to investigate slowdowns to Starlink and Starshield services, which Ukrainian officials said had hampered their ability to intercept Russian drones. The Trump administration and SpaceX have offered conflicting accounts of who was responsible.
Applebaum expects lawmakers to examine those disruptions further, along with the administration's negotiations with Russia and Ukraine, including allegations of business dealings involving negotiators.
She expects those issues to become "more open, more part of the conversation, more part of criticism."

articles.title_orig: No, ‘mogging’ does not signal the decline of the English language
articles.title_zh: No, ‘mogging’ does not signal the decline of the English language
articles.content_orig:
The Collins English Dictionary announced its 2026 word of the year Tuesday morning, with judges opting for “mogging.”
For readers not fluent in youth culture: Mogging “might involve making [anyone] look inferior in terms of appearance, confidence or status — anything, really,” according to marketing consultant and copywriter Rachel Quin, who authored a Collins article announcing the winner.
According to Collins, the term originated in the bodybuilding community as a shortening of AMOG (“alpha male of the group”) and penetrated into the so-called manosphere , a collection of typically online male communities united by their beliefs about masculinity.
“Fast forward to 2026 and it’s everywhere,” Quin added. And, crucially for POLITICO’s purposes, it can be applied to literally any situation.
With that in mind, we looked back at five top political moggings in 2026 — the more brutal, the better.
One minute, Keir Starmer was British prime minister with a thumping Labour majority cheering his every move. The next, he was humiliated and ousted by a northern rival who had done little to hide his own leadership ambitions.
Starmer, of course, tried to block the Downing Street takeover by Manchester Mayor Andy Burnham.
But once Burnham loyalists and grumpy ministers had quit Starmer’s government in droves, the prime minister bowed out this summer after just two years in office and Burnham — having manufactured, at the second attempt, an opportunity to enter parliament — waltzed into the top job unopposed.
Call it the textbook framemog.
Mozambique’s towering president, Daniel Chapo — who stands more than two meters tall — loomed over tiny Russian leader Vladimir Putin at a summit between African countries and Russia in Moscow last week.
Countries signed a summit declaration pledging to expand “cooperation in energy, minerals, and digital technology, establishing Russian industrial zones in Africa, and localizing production” — but the defining image of the summit was a photo of Chapo dwarfing Putin .
Looksmaxxing influencer Clavicular, real name Braden Peters, likely breathed a sigh of relief, having suffered the year’s other most notorious framemogging, at the hands of internet character “ASU frat leader.”
In a classic case of nominative determinism, Jacob Rees-Mogg, former British government minister and current haunted pencil, pantsed American commentator Tucker Carlson in a discussion on the latter’s YouTube channel in October.
Rees-Mogg may not have expected to find himself defending Britain’s decision to fight against Adolf Hitler, but that’s what happened after Carlson questioned why Britain had even bothered entering World War II against Nazi Germany.
Rees-Mogg said he was very surprised that Carlson was “verging on defending Hitler,” adding: “I think this is not really what you want to be doing,” in a clip that went viral and catapulted the Brexit hard-liner back into the British public consciousness.
Donald Trump’s bid to clean out the iconic Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in Washington, D.C. was initially hampered by persistent pond scum.
After a money-spinning renovation in early summer, algae came back with a vengeance, turning the water green and murky, while the blue paint job began to peel off the pool bottom.
Rather than turn his ire toward the contractors, Trump blamed vandals for attacking the pool, and his Department of Justice attempted to prosecute people it accused of damaging the site. Judges, however, dropped or dismissed the criminal cases.
Trump returned to the theme Monday — right before America went to the polls for midterm elections in which the country is laser-focused on the surging cost of living and corruption — holding a rally in front of the pool and recounting all the issues he said he’d fixed with the pool, including “tremendous algae.”
In Hungary’s biggest aura battle ever , conservative challenger Péter Magyar defeated longtime nationalist leader Viktor Orbán, ending 16 years in power for the populist prime minister.
Magyar, a former MP for Orbán’s Fidesz party, dramatically broke ranks in 2024, releasing a tape of his ex-wife apparently incriminating members of Orbán’s inner circle in a corruption scandal when she was justice minister. For two years, he consistently attacked Fidesz and Orbán over graft while building a movement to take down the EU’s problem child.
Magyar ultimately led a big-tent campaign focusing on cost-of-living concerns and pro-EU messaging, which turned into a landslide election victory that left Trump and the Kremlin salty .

articles.title_orig: Six Pallets of NVIDIA Hardware Worth $11.4 Million Stolen on the Way to Texas
articles.title_zh: Six Pallets of NVIDIA Hardware Worth $11.4 Million Stolen on the Way to Texas
articles.content_orig:
OAKLAND, Calif. (KGO) -- Authorities are investigating the theft of more than $11 million worth of Nvidia computer hardware in Oakland, in what experts describe as a sophisticated cargo heist targeting one of the world's most valuable technology companies.
According to reporting by the Bay Area News Group, the theft involved $11.4 million worth of Nvidia cargo that disappeared after departing Oakland on its way to Texas.
The shipment, consisting of six pallets of Nvidia hardware, left Oakland on Aug. 29 and was bound for Fort Worth, Texas. Authorities said the cargo was picked up as planned by a truck identified as a food transport company.
Investigators later lost track of the vehicle in San Bernardino County.
In a statement, Oakland police said: "The Oakland Police Department is investigating a grand theft that occurred in East Oakland. The victim reported the crime to OPD on September 13, 2026."
Olaf Groth, a professor at UC Berkeley's Haas School of Business and has expertise in artificial intelligence, emerging technology and global economics, said Nvidia chips are highly sought after.
"There's lots and lots of incentives to hijack those chips anywhere where security is weak," Groth said.
He said the chips can command significantly higher prices outside the United States.
"These chips command about double the price that they command inside the United States. So, if a chip costs about $550,000, then they go for about 1 million or more abroad," Groth said.
The theft is the latest in a series of crimes targeting high-value technology shipments in the Bay Area. Last year, police in Fremont and Union City investigated burglaries involving Nvidia cargo valued at more than $7.5 million.
Groth said the scale and complexity of such thefts suggest increasingly sophisticated criminal operations.
"Because the cargoes are getting bigger. The heists are getting more complex and that will point toward a professionalization of the teams that are hijacking these," he said.
An ABC7 viewer also provided video of a separate attempted theft in September. According to police, suspects believed they were targeting trucks carrying expensive Nvidia technology. The trucks instead contained 40,000 pounds of sand.
Groth said the incidents highlight broader concerns about protecting advanced computing technology.
"Security has to get a lot tighter around these because they're a national security asset," he said.
He also raised concerns about where stolen hardware could ultimately end up.
"This is a national security concern as well because we don't know where these chips are going. They could be going to China, they could be anywhere where we have conflict in the world," Groth said.
Authorities have not announced any arrests in the $11.4 million theft, and the investigation remains ongoing.
Experts say the case underscores growing concerns about the security of high-value technology shipments and the potential national security implications when advanced computer hardware enters the black market.

articles.title_orig: Poised for breakout moment in Latin America, Pope Leo also faces test of health
articles.title_zh: Poised for breakout moment in Latin America, Pope Leo also faces test of health
articles.content_orig:
ABOARD THE PAPAL FLIGHT — Three countries in 12 days, a dozen flights, two helicopter rides and nine Masses on a trip covering around 19,000 miles. Less than a month after Pope Leo XIV underwent cancer surgery , he set off on what the Vatican called a “homecoming” tour of South America.
The 71-year-old’s long trip across the strongly Catholic region will take him to Uruguay and Argentina, as well as to Peru, where he lived for decades and served as a bishop until 2023.
Leo considers the tour, one of the most grueling undertaken by a Catholic leader in decades, a “homecoming to places where he spent a long time and to which he feels closely connected,” Vatican spokesperson Matteo Bruni told journalists at a briefing Tuesday.
The Chicago-born pontiff, who is also a citizen of Peru, told pilgrims at his weekly audience in St. Peter’s Square on Wednesday that he was ⁠hoping to “strengthen the faith, renew hope” and “rekindle the fire of charity.”
Leo will hold several meetings with survivors of sexual abuse by ​Catholic clergy during the trip, the Vatican has said, without yet providing further details.
Bruni said the pope would also address a range of issues facing the continent, including environmental destruction, ⁠arms trafficking and regional political instability, bringing “a message of communion and unity.”
Leo departed from Rome’s Fiumicino Airport early ​Friday, and arrived in Uruguay on Friday afternoon for the country’s first papal visit since 1988.
After takeoff, Leo told journalists aboard the plane that he had no doubt he would embark on the trip.
“I know some people were doubtful about this trip taking place. I confess that from the first day I had no doubt,” he said. “I was convinced that this trip had to go forward and very happy to say, praise the Lord and thanks to wonderful medical assistants, I am here today, I think, in fairly good shape.”
Asked if he had any advice for other people facing cancer, Leo replied, “Not to be afraid, early detection is obviously the best way to go, regular check ups and take care of yourself.”
Leo also noted in response to a question from NBC News that “trust in God, good doctors, good surgeons, and, overall, a healthy lifestyle” had contributed to his quick recovery.
Leo, who is the first pope to vote in a U.S. election, was also asked about the importance of voting.
“I am proud to be an American and to exercise my right,” he said.
Considered the most secular country in the region, where only a fraction of people go to Mass regularly, Uruguay was the first in the world to legalize marijuana for recreational use and the second country in Latin America to decriminalize abortion.
In October 2025, the country of just 3.5 million people became the first in the region to approve legislation for assisted dying despite strong opposition from the Catholic Church.
After Uruguay, Leo’s tour will take him to Argentina for three days, where he is expected to meet with right-wing President Javier Milei , a close ally of President Donald Trump .
It will be the first papal visit to Argentina since Pope John Paul II traveled to the country in 1987.
Leo’s immediate predecessor, Pope Francis, was born in Argentina, the first pontiff from the region, but he declined numerous invitations to return to his homeland.
The biggest crowds of the trip are likely next week during his six-day visit to Peru, where Leo is widely celebrated as a beloved national figure. He will stop off in the capital, Lima, before visiting his former diocese of Chiclayo, where he was ordained bishop in 2014 and remained until taking up a Vatican post in 2023.
Leo, who was treated last month for lung ‌adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer, will also make several high-altitude visits in the Peruvian Andes.
Doctors have ⁠said that the disease was localized and that he would not require any further treatments; Bruni said Leo had recovered enough that no additional medical measures ⁠would be necessary during his trip.
Speaking at the same briefing Tuesday, Maria Montserrat Alvarado, the Vatican’s new communications chief, said Leo was grateful for the concern about his health and the demands the journey might make on him.
But, she said, he was “so excited” to make the trip.
Claudio Lavanga is Rome-based foreign correspondent for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: Elon Musk Staked His Empire on Texas. Now State Democrats Want to Rein Him In.
articles.title_zh: Elon Musk Staked His Empire on Texas. Now State Democrats Want to Rein Him In.
articles.content_orig:
SpaceX and Tesla shares declined by about 9% and 11%, respectively, on Thursday afternoon with investors concerned that Elon Musk could face new congressional probes — and his companies stricter regulation — following the U.S. midterm elections.
The declines, which correlated with a broader tech sell-off , brought aggregate market cap losses for SpaceX and Tesla to over $420 billion since Tuesday's close.
Musk's wealth, which had topped $1 trillion after SpaceX's initial public offering in June, is now down below $800 billion, having dropped about $90 billion in the past week, according to Forbes . He is still the richest man in the world.
Musk was the biggest donor to GOP candidates and causes in the midterms, with his financial contributions exceeding $470 million , the Financial Times first reported.
Despite his bolstering the GOP war chest, most of the candidates Musk backed lost their races .
Democrats won control of both the House and Senate. And in Texas, where both Tesla and SpaceX are headquartered, Democrats Sen.-elect James Talarico and Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa beat longtime Musk allies, state Attorney General Ken Paxton and Gov. Greg Abbott.
Deutsche Bank analysts wrote in a note out on Wednesday, "While policy is naturally hard to predict, we could envision SpaceX facing some incremental headwinds in this type of backdrop."
Gov.-elect Hinojosa "made data centers a major campaign issue," the analysts noted, calling for "a moratorium on new approvals until the legislature passes stronger protections on water use, electricity costs, local control, and incentives," and criticizing tax breaks for large facilities.
Tesla and SpaceX are both building out AI infrastructure in Texas, and are planning to build Terafab, a massive facility, which will include a data center and sprawling semiconductor factory, in Grimes County, Texas.
SpaceX also plans to build out a "supercomputer" at its Starbase, Texas, launch facility and company town, according to company job listings .
Deutsche Bank analysts also wrote that SpaceX's Texas compute capacity could now be at risk of delays. Capital expenditures by the company may need to increase to meet the requirements of tighter, anticipated regulations around data center buildout, the analysts wrote.
Musk and SpaceX have been instructed to preserve records concerning restrictions imposed on a military version of the Starlink satellite internet service in Ukraine, CNN first reported , citing an aide to a Democratic senator. The restrictions hampered the country's ability to defend against attacks by Russia.
Additionally, regulatory scrutiny could block chances for Musk to merge SpaceX and Tesla, an idea he has promoted, while acknowledging shareholders' approval would be required first.
SpaceX and Tesla had lost about $456 billion in market cap by the close of business on Thursday.
-- CNBC's Nick Wells contributed reporting.
