articles.title_orig: The Taipei Mayor Election Is Not About China - The Diplomat
articles.title_zh: The Taipei Mayor Election Is Not About China - The Diplomat
articles.content_orig:
In October, well-known Taiwanese television host Kevin Tsai, popular on both sides of the Taiwan Strait, was spotted by the media attending a campaign event for Puma Shen, a legislator running for mayor of Taipei. Given Tsai’s popularity in China, his appearance quickly sparked criticism. The incumbent Taipei mayor, Chiang Wan-an, helped defuse the controversy by inviting Tsai to the opening of his own campaign headquarters. Three weeks after attending Shen’s campaign event, Tsai publicly stated that he had never supported Taiwanese independence and that his work required him to interact with people holding a range of political views. The following day, he attended Chiang’s campaign event.
If attending a rally is tantamount to declaring one’s support for Taiwan’s future, imagine what will be made of the November 28 vote.
Shen, the candidate of the ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP), has spent years studying Chinese influence operations and promoting civilian preparedness in Taiwan. Chinese authorities have opened an investigation into him on allegations of secession. Chiang, the Kuomintang (KMT) incumbent, has maintained an open channel of communication between officials in Taipei and Shanghai. Beijing and Washington may be tempted to interpret a Shen victory as a vote for independence or a Chiang victory as a turn toward China. Either interpretation, however, would link a municipal election to an issue that Taipei’s voters have not been asked to vote on.
Consider an exchange during the October 31 debate between Shen and Chiang. Chiang challenged Shen to explain why two redevelopment projects, one in Datong and the other in Neihu, had stalled. Chiang attributed the delays to restrictions on building heights near Taipei’s Songshan Airport. Shen fired back with a question of his own: If city officials knew about these restrictions, why hadn’t they explained them to residents from the outset? Chiang used the exchange to question his challenger’s command of city affairs. Shen, in turn, used it to ask what good that expertise did residents if they learned about an obstacle too late to do anything about it.
The most important takeaway from their heated exchanges, however, is not what the candidates said, but what they left unsaid. China, the elephant in the room when it comes to cross-strait relations, was not raised even once as a key issue during the two-hour debate.
That encapsulates the kind of local issues Taipei voters will actually base their decision on. Some might vote for Chiang, crediting him with moving other difficult projects forward, including one at Nanjichang Night Market. Others might favor Shen’s proposal to screen older buildings for earthquake risks and to help residents arrange repairs. Two homeowners could vote for different candidates – while holding precisely the same views about China. The election night count offers no way to tell.
Taipei’s recent electoral history illustrates the limits of interpreting local elections through the lens of national politics – and vice versa. In 2022, the city elected Chiang as mayor. Just over a year later, in the presidential election, the DPP’s Lai Ching-te carried Taipei, edging out the KMT’s Hou Yu-ih by just 641 votes. Chiang’s mayoral victory would therefore have been a poor guide to the city’s presidential preferences. There is even less reason to interpret a vote in the capital as evidence of a broader change of heart across Taiwan for or against a political party – or that party’s approach to China.
True, the result will shape national politics. Winning Taipei would give Shen a larger audience for his work on civilian defense. A second term would give Chiang greater standing within the KMT to make the case for engagement with Shanghai, and possibly Beijing. Plus, the Taipei mayorship has in the past served as a launching pad for presidential ambitions. Winning office gives a politician the chance to advance causes that may have had little to do with why voters chose him.
The election’s outcome could certainly also influence cross-strait relations. During Chiang’s tenure, the Taipei–Shanghai Twin-City Forum has kept officials from the two cities in contact. A Chiang victory would give him another term to pursue those exchanges. A Shen victory would test the conditions under which they can continue. Although Shen has criticized the forum’s value, he has said he would attend if it offered practical benefits and came without political preconditions. On October 14, Beijing’s Taiwan Affairs Office dismissed his offer, citing his alleged support for independence.
Suppose Shen wins, repeats his offer, and finds Shanghai unwilling to meet with him. Concluding that Taipei voters chose to sever contact would erase Beijing’s role in the decision. The reverse inference – that vote for Chiang implies approval of his engagement with Chinese officials – would be equally questionable. A Taipei resident might value Chiang’s ability to keep municipal officials talking while still opposing closer political ties. Wanting the conversation with Shanghai to continue is entirely compatible with wanting Beijing to have less say in Taiwan’s affairs.
Local governance is undoubtedly important for the stability of the Taiwan Strait. Taipei’s city government, for example, helps residents prepare for an air raid, down to practicing how to reach shelter when the sirens sound. How well the city carries out that work matters regardless of which party holds power. Still, it’s not going to be an issue that is top of mind when Taipei residents fill out their ballots.
On November 28, Taipei’s voters will choose who takes responsibility for the safety of their homes, the city’s readiness for an emergency, and its dealings with Shanghai. Beijing and Washington have good reason to pay close attention to what the next mayor does with that authority. But anyone claiming a mandate for independence or unification is looking for evidence the mayoral count cannot provide.

articles.title_orig: Spain's rail authorities face European fraud probe after Urda rail disaster
articles.title_zh: Spain's rail authorities face European fraud probe after Urda rail disaster
articles.content_orig:
European Union prosecutors have begun investigating the possible misuse of EU funds meant for upgrading the Spanish railway line where a train crash killed 69 people last week.
Prosecutors backed by a special unit of Spain's Guardia Civil security force said they were conducting the inquiry at the offices of Adif rail infrastructure authority and rail safety agency AESF.
The 28 October accident on the Madrid-Seville high-speed line was one of the worst railway disasters in Europe this century.
It is the second EU fraud inquiry opened into Spain's railways this year, after 46 people were killed on the same line at Adamuz in January.
Last week, a train operated by state-owned operator Renfe ploughed into the back of a stationary train belonging to private Spanish company Iryo outside the village of Urda, around 130km (80 miles) south of Madrid.
The LZB communication system that monitors the position of trains had gone down, and the Renfe train had been given the all clear to start running at normal speed, even though the Iryo train ahead of it had been unable to restart.
The two accidents nine months apart on the same line have claimed 115 lives and dozens more injuries.
The European Public Prosecutor's Office (EPPO) said on Friday it had begun conducting investigative measures at Spain's rail authorities "after the opening of an investigation into possible fraud affecting EU funds allocated to the renovation and upgrading of safety, signalling and communications systems on the Madrid-Seville high-speed railway line".
The EPPO highlighted high public interest in the case, but said no further details would be made public.
As part of the process, a Spanish judge assigned to the case has to ensure the investigation complies with legal safeguards, including authorising any measures that might involve house searches or phone-tapping.
The Urda disaster has damaged the Socialist-led government of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez ahead of a 29 November general election and the party is trailing the conservative People's Party (PP) in most opinion polls.
Close Sánchez ally Óscar Puente resigned this week as transport minister, after seeing two deadly accidents on his watch this year.
The PP and far-right Vox say Puente's resignation is not enough and they have demanded that Sánchez resign too.
Many people in Spain have now become wary of taking the train, with reports of widespread cancellations and empty station platforms.
A funeral for the 69 victims at Urda will take place on Tuesday at Toledo cathedral, in the same province that the disaster happened.
Puente's successor, Carlos Cuerpo, has vowed to take all necessary measures to "restore the confidence of Spaniards in our high-speed rail".
Cuerpo met survivors of January's Adamuz disaster on Friday and they handed him a list of 11 demands for improving safety on Spain's railways.

articles.title_orig: US and Iran Edge Closer to Deal With Nuclear Issue Back in Play
articles.title_zh: US and Iran Edge Closer to Deal With Nuclear Issue Back in Play
articles.content_orig:
The office of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Friday that aid provided by the U.S. has been used by Israel "both to defend itself and to confront enemies who threaten America and the West."
"U.S. military aid to Israel has always been a cross-the-aisle agreement," the office wrote on X after President Donald Trump announced earlier this week that $4 billion in aid would be "cut off at the end of the year."
"Today, Israel has a strong and stable economy. The move by PM Netanyahu and President Trump from aid to partnership shows the strength and sophistication of our relationship, and its ability to adapt and stand strong over time," Netanyahu's office added.
Trump said on Election Day, "Israel's our number one," and, "We give them more than anybody else, and they no longer need it."
President Donald Trump said Friday that "Israel and, in fact, the entire Middle East, WOULD NOT EXIST TODAY if I did not stop Iran from having a Nuclear Weapon.
"Nobody wants to say that, but everybody knows it’s true!" the president added in a post on Truth Social.
Trump made the remark after announcing earlier this week that $4 billion in U.S. aid to Israel would be "cut off" by the end of the year.
An Iranian military official vowed Friday that any country helping the U.S. in a potential new attack on Iran would become a legitimate target, a report said.
Brig. Gen. Ali Balali, who is a senior advisor to the commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) Aerospace Force, also said Friday that Iran's missiles have enough range to strike U.S. and Israeli targets, according to Iran's Tasnim News Agency.
The remarks come after reports emerged last week that movements were being made in the Middle East to give President Donald Trump options if he decided to pursue further military action against Iran following Tuesday's midterm elections.
Russia played a larger role in the Iran war than previously disclosed, with internal defense industry documents revealing how Moscow built up the country's arsenal ahead of its conflict with the U.S.
A Russian contract is tied to 90 launchers for precision-guided missiles with the destination as Tehran, according to documents obtained and published by Ukrainian defense intelligence research group Dallas Analytics offering new details on the extent of Moscow's military support for Iran before war erupted.
President Donald Trump has repeatedly downplayed Russia's role in the conflict — as recently as last month, saying that he did not believe they are helping Iran "at all."
Russian production records show components were allocated for 90 APU-L twin-rail launchers under a contract identified as "K-10," with shipments within the Russian production chain scheduled from late 2024 through December 2025.
Other internal Russian documents obtained by Dallas Analytics explicitly identify "K-10" as Iran. An October 2022 supply request for equipment for a Yak-130 aircraft lists the consignee as "'K10' Iran" and was countersigned by the acting head of the Russian Defense Ministry's 704th Military Representation.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre (UKMTO) said Friday that eight ships have been attacked so far this week in the Strait of Hormuz.
Since July 6, a total of 63 of 88 projectile strikes happened along a southern route near the coastline of Oman, according to the UKMTO.
There were also three ships attacked this week in the Arabian Gulf, it added.
"Of the 11 incidents, 3 continued their voyage, 5 required assistance and 3 Vessels sunk," the UKMTO said in a weekly overview, noting that the risk for ships traveling through the Strait of Hormuz remains "severe."

articles.title_orig: Where China Sees the Danger in a Wounded Trump
articles.title_zh: Where China Sees the Danger in a Wounded Trump
articles.content_orig:
China won’t be so quick to celebrate the stunning blue wave that washed over President Donald Trump this week.
American voters may have withdrawn the Republican mandate by giving Democrats the keys to Congress, but Trump can still direct his executive powers abroad, even as the opposition prepares to restrain him at home.
After a bruising midterm result for the U.S. president, a wounded Trump may seem like easy pickings for Chinese leader Xi Jinping , who will soon send negotiators to restart trade talks designed to neutralize America’s long-term tariff threat.
Xi had an understanding with Trump and knew what made him tick. But the political setback may make Trump much harder to predict .
Xi spent considerable resources on his rapprochement with Trump, including a state media campaign about Chinese resilience that stopped hostile economic acts by the United States and resulted in two glitzy state visits this year.
A promise to meet Trump at the APEC summit in southern China later this month, and again when Miami hosts the G20 meeting in December, has helped Xi build certainty into China’s relations with its top geopolitical rival.
Beijing may even go as far as to give Trump a foreign policy win at APEC by agreeing to a three-way meeting with Russia’s President Vladimir Putin in host city Shenzhen. Whether Xi makes any concrete commitments there is another question.
“Stability” has been the watchword in China for years, but it has extra weight this year after a campaign of purges swept up dozens of senior figures in elite Chinese politics and the military. Xi’s purges are about corruption in the Chinese Communist Party , but they’re also about loyalty—to him.
A recent gathering of the CCP’s Central Committee had the lowest attendance in over half a century, hinting at the scale of disciplinary action taken ahead of the party’s 21 st national congress in 12 months’ time, when Xi is widely expected to win an uncontested fourth 5-year term.
“Xi’s main political goal now is to secure another term at the 21st Party Congress. That requires not only a firm grip on power but also a case that his continued rule is legitimate and natural,” wrote Christopher Nye, a senior fellow at the Jamestown Foundation think tank.
Xi used the latest gathering of party cadres “to resolve the problems of legitimacy created by the purge,” Nye wrote this week.
A fourth term could extend Xi’s rule over China to 20 years.
So, 2027 will be a delicate year for Xi. He’ll be wary of a Trump unleashed , who, despite being weakened domestically, could channel his energy into foreign policy matters, namely negotiations with China to extend or rip up the Busan truce that kept tariffs at a minimum in exchange for Chinese agricultural purchases and other key commitments.
“Beijing could conclude the election results mean Trump needs an economic agreement more than China does…. In that sense, Beijing could turn Trump’s political setback into a bargaining miscalculation that unsettles the very stability Xi is trying to preserve,” said Craig Singleton, senior director of the China program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies think tank.
“If Beijing expects last night’s result to humble Trump, it is probably mistaken. He may have less room politically at home, but that could produce even bolder executive action abroad, including new pressure on Chinese companies, tighter economic-security measures and faster reshoring.
"Beijing should be careful about mistaking Trump’s political weakness for restraint in his China policy ."
Trump’s first presidency also began with personal diplomacy with China’s Xi before flattery gave way to full-blown systemic confrontation.
Trump hosted Xi at Mar-a-Lago in spring 2017 and Xi returned the favor in fall with a lavish state visit for Trump in Beijing. The two leaders appeared to agree on $250 billion in commercial deals, which later never materialized.
The trade war followed in 2018, along with the first stage of the tech war that targeted Chinese telecoms giant Huawei the following year. The Phase One trade deal in early 2020 eased tensions but didn’t stop them from boiling over once more during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Beijing was so concerned by the downturn in relations and the mixed signals out of the White House that it feared an “ October surprise ,” a military strike to rally support before Trump’s presidential race with Democrat Joe Biden.
Gen. Mark Milley, then chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, called his Chinese counterpart without Trump’s knowledge to assure him that the U.S. government was planning no such action—and to preempt any miscalculation by Beijing.
Trump’s last experience as a lame duck president didn’t lead to a hot war, but it locked in a new Cold War with China, one of economic decoupling and export controls. And on the last full day of the first Trump administration, his then secretary of state, Mike Pompeo, accused Xi’s government of genocide against Muslims in far-western China.
On the day Biden took office as the new U.S. president, China sanctioned former senior Trump officials in retaliation for the wild final weeks. The message to the new administration, and indeed the expectation, was that Trump’s hard-line China policies should be walked back. That didn’t happen and the rivalry was institutionalized.
Trump has no reason to hold back if Xi doesn’t play ball. And even with Trump neutered, the Democrats may not play nice.

articles.title_orig: Taiwan to close representative office in Papua New Guinea, blames China
articles.title_zh: Taiwan to close representative office in Papua New Guinea, blames China
articles.content_orig:
Taiwan says it is closing its representative office in Papua New Guinea and will stop buying liquefied natural gas (LNG) from the country, blaming Chinese political pressure on the South Pacific nation.
Taiwan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said on Friday that Papua New Guinea had repeated previous demands that staff leave its office in the capital, Port Moresby, within a set deadline and had pushed for ⁠its closure.
These actions “reflect China’s continued use of political pressure and economic influence to interfere in other countries’ diplomatic decisions and suppress Taiwan’s international space”, it said in a statement.
China, which claims Taiwan as part of its territory, had welcomed Papua New Guinea’s decision in July to shutter Taiwan’s office in Port Moresby. Taipei rejected the move, and the office remained open in the interim.
The Pacific has long been an area for diplomatic competition between China and Taiwan. Papua New Guinea has formal diplomatic relations with China, but it had allowed Taiwan to have a representative office in Port Moresby.
Taiwan has formal diplomatic ties with only three Pacific Islands nations: Palau, Tuvalu and the Marshall Islands. It also has a representative office in Fiji. Just 12 countries maintain formal ⁠diplomatic ties with Taiwan.
Taiwan previously announced that it had stopped spot purchases of LNG from the South Pacific nation, but on Friday the ministry said it also would no longer sign new spot purchase contracts with the country.
Taiwanese LNG purchases accounted for one-third of Papua New Guinea’s exports.
Last year, Taiwan imported about 8 percent of its natural gas from Port Moresby.
Taipei will also end technical cooperation and assistance programmes, “including medical missions, related scholarship and talent development programmes”, the ministry said.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic IPO Buyers See Valuation as Low as $1.1 Trillion
articles.title_zh: Anthropic IPO Buyers See Valuation as Low as $1.1 Trillion
articles.content_orig:
Following tech's selloff on Wall Street this week, some investors are lowering their expectations for Anthropic.
The artificial intelligence company had been looking toward a $2 trillion valuation in its IPO up until recently, but stakeholders told CNBC that even $1.5 trillion is now in doubt, with one investor calling that number a "stretch."
Anthropic declined to comment.
The change in sentiment comes alongside growing concerns about the outsized spending by AI companies and a sharp post-midterm slump in the market. The Nasdaq plummeted more than 5% on Thursday, its steepest drop in 19 months, reflecting fears that Democrats' newfound power in Washington, D.C., and a nationwide rebuke of AI will lead to a slowdown in the buildout of data centers.
Bearishness on the AI trade was on the rise before the election. The Nasdaq suffered its worst month in October since March 2025, led by declines in chipmakers and neoclouds.
Anthropic is set to list on the Nasdaq , under the ticker ANT, and is gearing up for an expected debut in a matter of weeks. Last month, Anthropic was reportedly seeking a valuation as high as $2 trillion . As of May, the company was privately valued at $965 billion.
With the latest market turmoil, one investor said $1 trillion to $1.25 trillion is a more likely valuation target, although that could change with market conditions. The investors asked not to be named because they're not authorized to speak about the matter.
Gil Luria, an analyst at D.A. Davidson, told CNBC that, "Investors will expect the IPO to be priced at least at the low end of previous expectations."
"The market really needs this IPO to go well and the bankers on the deal surely understand that," Luria said. "The best way to set Anthropic up for success is to price the deal well."
The company is expected to kick off its roadshow next week.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic IPO announcement odds drop on Kalshi following midterms and AI sell-off
articles.title_zh: Anthropic IPO announcement odds drop on Kalshi following midterms and AI sell-off
articles.content_orig:
Odds that Anthropic will announce a public offering fell in recent days on Kalshi as AI-related stocks slid after Democrats won control of Congress and several key governorships.
In the last week, odds that Anthropic would announce an IPO before December fell to 57% from over 85% on Kalshi. Chances that the company would announce a public offering before January also dropped to 68% from 90% in the last week. The contract asks when Anthropic will officially announce an IPO and will be verified by news outlets.
The AI company confidentially filed its IPO prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission back in June.
The repricing on Kalshi came as investors grew concerned that Democratic victories across both chambers could slow data center construction, making the bet on AI less attractive.
Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa of Texas, a Democrat who ousted three-term Republican Greg Abbott, championed tighter protocols against data center buildout in her state during her campaign.
"We will have laws to protect Texans and we need to stop what we are doing with data centers until we have those protections," the Democrat told CNN on Thursday.
The Nasdaq Composite closed Thursday more than 10% below its most recent high, crossing the benchmark for what Wall Street views as a correction. The S&P 500 lost 4.4%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell more than 1,800 points, or 3.4%. Stocks were attempting to rebound on Friday, with the Nasdaq gaining 1.3% and the S&P 500 rising 0.7%. The Dow shed 0.2%.
On Friday, shares of Micron Technology and Nvidia each gained about 4%, after falling 17% and 9%, respectively, the day before. CoreWeave shares also rose more than 2% Friday morning after tumbling about 10% on Wednesday. Even if Friday's gains are sustained, these stocks have tallied steep losses over the past week.

articles.title_orig: US economy adds 165,000 jobs in October, blowing past expectations
articles.title_zh: US economy adds 165,000 jobs in October, blowing past expectations
articles.content_orig:
Kenny Polcari discusses the historical S&P 500 performance following midterm elections. He predicts the stock market will be higher in 12 months, continuing a trend seen in every midterm cycle since World War II.
The U.S. economy added jobs at a strong pace in October, rebounding from a softer September amid economic uncertainty.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics on Friday reported that employers added 165,000 jobs in October. That figure was well above the 65,000 estimate of economists polled by LSEG.
The unemployment rate decreased slightly to 4.1%, which was lower than the expectations of economists who predicted it would hold steady at 4.2%.
Revisions were made to the payroll numbers for the prior two months, with August revised up by 53,000 from a gain of 133,000 jobs to 186,000 jobs; while the change for September was revised up by 31,000 jobs from a gain of 29,000 to 60,000.
Taken together, employment in August and September was 84,000 higher than previously reported.
TRUMP ADMIN NAMES NEW ECONOMIC OPPORTUNITY ZONES TO SPUR PRIVATE INVESTMENT IN STRUGGLING COMMUNITIES
Private payrolls grew by 159,000 jobs in October, well above the 64,000 expected by economists polled by LSEG.
Government payrolls increased by 6,000 jobs in October. The sector's loss of 17,000 jobs in September was revised down to a loss of 18,000 jobs. The federal government shed 1,000 jobs in October, while state governments added 8,000 jobs and local governments cut 1,000 roles last month.
The manufacturing sector added 19,000 jobs in October, well above the gain of 5,000 that was predicted by economists polled by LSEG. September's gain of 9,000 jobs was also revised up to 13,000. Professional and business services added 70,000 jobs in October, which was well above the average monthly gain of 15,000 jobs over the past 12 months. The sector's job growth was led by gains in professional, scientific and technical services (+32,900), and in administrative and support and waste management and remediation services (+28,100).
Healthcare added 41,600 jobs in October, above the average monthly gain of 31,000 over the last 12 months. Most of last month's gains were in hospitals (+16,000), home healthcare services (+10,500) and outpatient care centers (+4,800).
Transportation and warehousing added 24,800 jobs last month, with growth occurring among couriers and messengers (+17,400) and air transportation (+3,500).
Private payrolls grew by 159,000 in October, well above the expectations of a gain of 64,000 jobs. (Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
PRIVATE SECTOR ADDED 86,000 JOBS IN OCTOBER, ABOVE EXPECTATIONS, ADP SAYS
The number of long-term unemployed, defined as those who have been jobless for 27 weeks or more, was 2 million in October and changed little over the month. The long-term unemployed accounted for 27.6% of all unemployed people.
The number of people employed part-time for economic reasons rose by 339,000 to 4.8 million in October. These individuals would've preferred full-time work but were working part-time because their hours were reduced, or they were unable to find full-time jobs.
The labor force participation was 61.9% in October, while the employment-population ratio was 59.3%. Both of these figures were little changed in October and have shown little net change since January.
Average hourly earnings increased 3.1% year over year in October, above the 2.4% rise predicted by LSEG economists. Earnings also grew 0.4% on a monthly basis, above the 0.3% estimate in the LSEG poll.
FED'S PREFERRED INFLATION GAUGE ROSE IN SEPTEMBER AS THIRD-QUARTER GDP BEATS EXPECTATIONS
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh and central bank policymakers will hold their next interest rate meeting on December 8-9. (Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Seema Shah, chief global strategist at Principal Asset Management, said in a statement that the October jobs report "is a strong rebuttal to fears that the economy is heading into a meaningful slowdown."
"Payrolls growth surprised firmly to the upside, unemployment fell back to 4.1%, and job creation remains broad-based, pointing to an economy that is still absorbing labor comfortably rather than one beginning to buckle under tighter financial conditions," Shah said. "With wage growth also picking up, a December Fed hike remains firmly on the table despite the recent tightening in financial conditions."
Lindsay Rosner, head of multi-sector fixed income investing at Goldman Sachs Asset Management, said that the October jobs report's "payroll number removed the traffic light at the December intersection for the Fed."
"Fed focus was already firmly on moderating inflation , and continued signs of tightening in the labor market give it a license to raise rates without hindering its employment mandate. Additional tightening is possible in the first quarter if inflation continues to print strong," Rosner added.
The strong October jobs report raised the likelihood of the Federal Reserve hiking interest rates when it holds its next meeting on Dec. 8-9.
The market's expectations of a 25-basis-point rate hike ticked up on Friday, with the CME FedWatch tool showing a 76.8% probability the Fed hikes in December – an increase from 66.9% a week ago. A hike of that size would take the federal funds rate to a target range of 4% to 4.25%.

The benchmark S&P 500 Index rose 0.65% during Friday morning's trading session.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 0.2%, while the Nasdaq Composite rose 1.25%.

articles.title_orig: Europe alarmed by US plans for security deal with Russia
articles.title_zh: Europe alarmed by US plans for security deal with Russia
articles.content_orig:
BRUSSELS — Europe is once again watching the White House through gritted teeth.
An opaque Trump administration proposal for a new European-wide security arrangement with Russia has met skepticism from European capitals that fear it risks sidelining the continent and emboldening Kremlin chief Vladimir Putin.
“We already have a European security architecture in place — NATO and European Union both have their respective roles,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Friday in reaction to the U.S. plan. “We must make sure Ukraine is integrated into this architecture. The problem remains that Russia keeps breaking the treaties that underpin it ... Putin does not have a veto over European security.”
The latest U.S. proposal underscores growing anxiety around Trump’s fresh rapprochement with Russia as he ramps up pressure on Ukraine and his administration attempts to revive long-stalled talks to end Moscow’s full-scale war against Kyiv.
POLITICO spoke to 12 NATO diplomats, EU envoys and European government officials, all of whom were granted anonymity to speak freely on the sensitive issue. NATO allies were not briefed about the American plans in advance, according to three alliance diplomats, and many remain skeptical of the idea.
U.S. President Donald Trump late Thursday talked of a “big, beautiful agreement,” after meeting with Putin’s envoy Kirill Dmitriev, adding: “It’s going to involve more than Ukraine, and I could even say it might involve all of Europe.”
“Our objective is to develop practical arrangements that address the security concerns of all sides, reduce the risk of future conflict, and create a more stable and predictable security environment,” Trump’s son-in-law and envoy Jared Kushner added soon after.
Kushner said the arrangement would have five goals: “Permanent security consultations, reliable crisis communications, greater military transparency, reciprocal measures to reduce escalation risks, and an enduring framework for long-term European security and stability.”
“It is a bit obscure what Kushner meant,” said one NATO diplomat. “The general sentiment in Europe is that any discussion with Russia on the future architecture at the moment will just be used by Moscow to legitimize their arguments ... it will not fly with the European allies.”
A senior European official added: “Literally, there’s nothing to find fault with, but we know there’s something else going on.”
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s top adviser, Björn Seibert, briefed EU ambassadors on Friday, according to two EU diplomats, following a discussion between national security advisers on the issue.
“There’s willingness to engage in Kyiv and in the rest of Europe although there’s little confidence in the Russians — but the EU is not blocking it,” one of the EU diplomats said after the meeting. But “the group around Trump underestimated how important the conflict is for Europe and how a bad outcome for Ukraine is very dangerous for Europe.”
“It's a long-standing position for us and many others that European security architecture should not be discussed while there is a war,” said a senior European security official. “And obviously not without Europeans.”
“Europe must have a seat at the table in negotiations on peace in Ukraine and the future European security architecture,” Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda added Friday, after a meeting of the eight Nordic and Baltic countries.
This week saw two rounds of working-level meetings in Brussels on a Ukraine peace deal, ahead of U.S.-brokered working-level talks with Ukraine and Russia on Nov. 10-11 in Abu Dhabi.
“We must be realistic about the peace talks and we must be very careful when it comes to the real intentions of Russia,” Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk told a group of reporters, including from POLITICO, earlier this week. “In winter, Putin might have less incentives to get a deal.”
Stefan Kornelius, spokesperson for German Chancellor Friedrich Merz — who talked to Trump on Thursday night — said: “A new sense of urgency has ... emerged” on negotiations after this week's U.S. midterm elections, adding the issue would resurface at an informal gathering of EU leaders in Dublin next week.
The meeting had been intended to focus on AI, but developments in Ukraine could overshadow the talks, a third EU diplomat said. “Things are moving pretty fast,” they said.
Still, some allies fear the U.S. may tie its new initiative to an upcoming review of American troops in Europe, expected in December.
“That’s the elephant in the room,” said a second NATO diplomat. “One thing is talking about European security architecture ... with an ‘ordinary’ U.S. posture; another thing is to talk about a European security architecture ‘as things will be,’ and nobody knows how that’ll be.”

articles.title_orig: US job growth exceeds expectations in October despite economic uncertainty
articles.title_zh: US job growth exceeds expectations in October despite economic uncertainty
articles.content_orig:
‘Low-hire, low-fire’ labor market shows sluggish growth but few layoffs, with an interest rate hike expected in December
The US added 165,000 jobs to the economy in October, a sign of resilience in the labor market amid ongoing war in the Middle East and inflation, according to new data released on Friday.
Economists had said the labor market has been stuck in a “low-hire, low-fire” state, in which job growth is sluggish but layoffs also remain low, but October’s data surpassed economist expectations. The unemployment rate went down slightly to 4.1%, the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) reported.
Average hourly earnings increased at an annual rate of 3.1%, slightly higher than last month. Inflation over the last few months has largely outpaced the growth in wages – what often leads people to feel they are spending even more to buy essentials. In September, the annualized inflation rate was 3.7%.
Initial figures for August and September were also revised up by a total of 84,000 jobs. Job growth was seen in healthcare, transportation, warehousing and manufacturing.
Other data released earlier this week showed employment has been steady. Layoffs in September fell to their lowest level in a year and a half, according to the bureau, while outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas tracked just under 44,000 layoffs in October – a 71% decrease compared with last October.
The new data comes after a seismic midterm election that solidified Democrats’ control of Congress for the next two years. Multiple polls had shown Americans were most frustrated about the state of the economy, especially higher gas and grocery prices.
“Americans delivered a clear verdict in the midterm elections that the current economy is squeezing people financially and making it hard to get by, let alone get ahead,” said Heather Long, chief economist at the Navy Federal Credit Union, in a statement before Friday’s report. “The labor market is a good example of why people are frustrated.”
But it’s unclear when Americans will get relief. Gas prices are on average $1 a gallon higher than they were a year ago because of the war in Iran. The price of diesel, which is used throughout the supply chain to power large vehicles, is 60% higher compared with prewar levels.
In times of stubborn inflation, the US Federal Reserve usually intervenes by raising interest rates, which slows price increases. In September, the Fed hiked interest rates for the first time since 2023, bringing them up to a range of 3.75%-4%, citing inflation. Though officials kept rates steady at their last meeting in October, held the week before the election, economists are expecting one more rate hikes at the next central bank meeting in December.
Meanwhile, markets over the last week have been shaken as investors appeared worried about AI spending. After reaching correction territory, when an index drops 10% below its most recent peak, the tech-heavy Nasdaq index briefly made a recovery on Wednesday before diving back into correction territory on Thursday.

articles.title_zh: After a $2.5 Trillion Wipeout, Tech Investors Brace for More Pain
articles.content_orig:

E very silver lining has a cloud, if you’ll pardon the pun. And so the unexpected Democrat “blue tsunami” that swept the US midterms has apparently exacerbated the big tech sell-off that has been quietly rumbling for some time, albeit until now not attracting many headlines outside the financial pages .
Trillions of dollars have been wiped off the stock value of major tech firms overnight in the US, Europe and Asia amid concerns of a slowdown in AI development.
There are fears that a Democrat-controlled Congress and newly installed blue governors in states such as Texas will pass laws, impose regulations and generally stymie the previously uninhibited growth in returns from already bloated AI investment.
If lawmakers won’t let the likes of OpenAI, X and Anthropic regulate themselves, and if state legislators won’t permit data centres to be built where residents don’t want them, then the industry will grow more slowly and generate lower profits. Therefore there’s less point in putting investors’ cash into them.
Hence what is now a general “correction” – a broad loss of about 10 per cent of value – rather than a crash. There’s still enough faith in the future of AI for it to attract investors who don’t want to be left with outdated portfolios – a useful “Fomo” effect. But there is also sufficient nerves, ignorance and lack of transparency around these new tech giants, AI itself, chipmakers and hardware firms, that valuations and share prices will be volatile.
We’ve seen such gyrations before, notably in the internet dot-com boom and crash around 2000, but also in previous over-excited booms such as railway mania of the 19th century. The good news is that although some investors are ruined, such over-exuberance leaves behind a socially useful legacy and some sound companies. This time, the scale of the money involved is unprecedented, so, as with the mooted flotation of Anthropic, a scaling back from $2 trillion to $1.5 trillion has an oversized impact. The same goes for ChatGPT , which has reduced a routine round of private fundraising from $30bn to $20bn. Another factor is the way highly leveraged hedge funds have piled in, drawing on private equity – and have all been placing their bets in the same direction.
They’ve also been running into trouble. There is also a significant Chinese sector, which, ironically, has many more publicly quoted AI companies than the US, based on an open access model. In New York, the only real examples are Alphabet, which owns Google and much else, plus Elon Musk’s SpaceX . Some disappointing numbers from Google the other day triggered a substantial fall in the share price, an early harbinger of the current turmoil. In any case, the average punter can get immediate exposure to the AI boom much more easily in China, which has its downsides when things get rocky. Out in Hong Kong, the Hang Seng Tech index, comprising 30 major technology companies, is down 30 per cent year to date.
Boom and bust then, which is normal for capitalism. But central banks and governments, at least in most of the West, will now find it extremely difficult to insulate their wider economies from a crash. This is something that Andrew Bailey , governor of the Bank of England, has been warning about, rightly, for some time. The problem now is that the levels of public debt and interest rates make it harder for the authorities to intervene to prevent a sectoral collapse from transmuting into a global recession. We were able to launch a massive international rescue campaign when the banks failed during the global financial crisis in 2008 and after.
The crash of 1987 was swiftly ameliorated by the Fed – the “Greenspan Put”, which has reassured market players in succeeding decades. Much the same goes for the aftershocks in the eurozone crises around 2011, bailed out by German public money, and we even managed to stop Covid from turning into a Great Recession by mortgaging our economies, borrowing a year’s worth of GDP. This time around, because we have less room for manoeuvre, it’s harder to see how the wider world economy can be cushioned from a tech sell-off that could easily turn into a panic, wiping billions off the value of people’s pensions, among other terrible consequences, as Donald Trump has rather gleefully pointed out. China and America won’t cooperate for geopolitical reasons, and Europe is irrelevant. So we find ourselves in the strange position that AI will ruin us before it makes us all rich, and we mere humans can’t understand why.

articles.title_orig: Russia to UAE, Iran steps up diplomacy amid Trump threats: What we know
articles.title_zh: Russia to UAE, Iran steps up diplomacy amid Trump threats: What we know
articles.content_orig:
Iran has stepped up diplomatic efforts amid suggestions by United States President Donald Trump that the US could resume full-scale strikes on Iran.
The US news website Axios quoted a US official saying that US Central Command (CENTCOM) was preparing for the resumption of major military operations in Iran, and that it was just waiting on orders from Washington. On Thursday, Trump told reporters the US may have to “destroy” the rest of Iran, adding that people will “know soon enough” if he acts.
Tehran’s intensified diplomatic push comes after Iran downed two US reconnaissance drones near Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, which the US struck earlier this week. Iran says it will retaliate if the US resumes larger strikes.
On Thursday, Iran offered the US a new nuclear and peace proposal via Qatari mediators, to be discussed only after Washington meets Tehran’s seven demands, a senior Iranian official told Reuters. The US is examining the proposal, Reuters reported.
Iran has made meeting its seven demands a condition for reopening the Strait of Hormuz and restarting peace talks, including on its nuclear programme. The demands include the lifting of sanctions on Iran, the unfreezing of Iranian assets and the end to the US naval blockade of its ports in and around the Strait of Hormuz, among other things.
It has also stepped up ties with Russia, with its top security official, Mohsen Rezaei, travelling to Moscow for talks on Thursday. During that visit, Rezaei said: “On the issue of diplomacy, we have announced seven conditions ⁠to the Americans. As long as they do ⁠not execute our seven conditions, we will neither open the Strait of Hormuz nor have negotiations.”
Meanwhile, the US has insisted a deal on Iran’s nuclear capacity must be part of any ceasefire agreement before wider peace talks can restart.
On Thursday, Rezaei met with Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Kremlin to deliver a message from Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei. Iranian state media did not elaborate on ⁠the contents of the message.
Rezaei called it “an extremely important exchange” according to remarks reported by the Iranian embassy, but also did not give further details.
However, The Financial Times reported that Russia previously agreed to supply Iran with 90 helicopter-mounted launchers for precision-guided missiles, despite needing its own weapons for the Ukraine war. The newspaper cited a Russian defence manufacturer’s production schedule for 2024 and 2025, which it has examined, showing an order for helicopter-mounted launchers being assigned a code used to refer to Iran in Russian defence documents.
Relations between Russia and Iran have deepened since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and during the US-Israeli war on Iran that saw the two countries become the most heavily sanctioned in the world. Iran has provided Shahed drones, which Russia has modified and used heavily against Ukraine.
In return, Russia has also reportedly helped Iran develop supersonic cruise missiles, sold it Verba shoulder-launched anti-air missiles and shared information with Tehran potentially relevant to nuclear weapons.
“It is indicative of Russia’s willingness to continue supplying Iran despite its own wartime demands and with far less concern about Western objections than in the past,” Nicole Grajewski, a non-resident scholar at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, told the FT.
In early October, Putin said Russia was prepared to take part in mediation to bring an end to the war .
Images released by the Kremlin showed its foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov and chief of the Russian military intelligence, Igor Kostyukov, attending a meeting with Iran’s security chief alongside Putin.
The meeting also strengthened Iran’s economic ties with Russia.
“During the meeting with Mr Vladimir Putin, discussions were held regarding the construction of gas pipelines from Russia to Iran,” said Rezaei, Iranian state TV reported.
He said the gas pipelines would address Iran’s gas shortages and facilitate the sale of Russian energy to neighbouring countries.
Tehran said Iran’s natural gas refineries had been hit during the most intense phase of US-Israeli strikes on Iran earlier this year, which lasted 40 days.
Separately, Russia’s Foreign Ministry advised citizens against travel to Iran “In light of the remaining risks of a new escalation around Iran”.
During the most intense fighting of the war, Iran struck bases in Gulf countries hosting US military assets, as well as civil and energy facilities and infrastructure.
Senior Iranian officials have repeatedly warned that any state helping the US to target the Islamic republic will be a “legitimate target” should US attacks resume.
On Thursday, Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi held phone calls with several Gulf leaders, including the foreign minister of the UAE, Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan.
They discussed regional developments as well as diplomatic efforts for stability in the region, according to Araghchi’s Telegram channel.
Araghchi spoke with Saudi Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud about efforts to improve security and stability in the region, according to the Saudi foreign ministry.
Araghchi also discussed de-escalation efforts with the foreign ministers of Kuwait and Turkiye.
In a separate call, Araghchi talked with Qatar’s Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani about coordinating to reduce tensions, the Qatari foreign ministry said.
Sheikh Mohammed stressed support for efforts to secure freedom of maritime navigation.
In a statement, Oman’s foreign ministry said the safety of passage through the Strait of Hormuz was a main topic of discussions, in a call between Araghchi and Oman’s foreign minister.
Iran continues to tightly control shipping lanes through the strait, where several ships have been damaged in recent days. It has granted exemptions to shipping restrictions to Iraq and Qatar, in the Gulf region, as well as to India and China.
Despite his Republican Party suffering a drubbing in this week’s US midterm elections – largely because of public anger over the war on Iran and the resulting rise in energy prices – US President Donald Trump has refused to rule out further strikes on Iran.
On Thursday, Trump told reporters at the Oval Office that he may have to “destroy the rest” of Iran.
Former Iranian diplomat Hadi Afghahi told Al Jazeera that Tehran can ease the path to a settlement if the US also shows flexibility. He argued that Trump “really does not want to go to war, because war again will cost him more”. However, the US president’s next move is unpredictable, observers say.
Afghahi cautioned that Trump “is still surrounded by a group of hawks”, including the energy and treasury secretaries.
Trump has shown willingness to engage in diplomacy, however. Qatar’s ⁠Emir ⁠Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad ⁠Al Thani discussed diplomatic ⁠efforts to ease regional tensions in a ‌phone call with Trump on Friday, according to the Qatari Emiri Diwan.
The leaders reviewed international diplomatic efforts, including the Doha-led mediation efforts to support negotiations in recent weeks, in a bid to reach “a comprehensive agreement that puts an end to the crisis”, the Diwan said in a statement.
Tehran warned it will retaliate on a wider scale than it has done so far if the US resumes the war. It has also said talks will become unfeasible.
Iranian officials said Iran has the capacity to strike further than the Gulf using weapons manufactured in Iran.
On Thursday, a spokesman for the Supreme Advisor to the Commander of the Aerospace Force of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said: “In the event of a new aggression, any country or force that helps America attack Iran can be a legitimate target of the Islamic Republic.”
